definition: The process by which banks transform the attributes of customer claims – duration, divisibility, liquidity, credit risk, and currency – by holding assets that differ from their liabilities along these dimensions. Long-term mortgages funded by short-term deposits is the canonical example. QAT is the source of both banks' economic value and their inherent fragility.
flashcardBack: Banks transform claim attributes (duration, divisibility, liquidity, credit risk, currency) by holding assets that differ from liabilities along these dimensions.

definition: A short-term borrowing arrangement in which one party sells securities to another with a contractual agreement to repurchase them at a higher price on a specified future date. Economically equivalent to a collateralised loan. The difference between the sale price and the repurchase price represents the interest. Repos are the primary funding instrument of shadow banking and were central to the 2007–09 crisis when haircuts spiked and repo markets froze.
flashcardBack: Collateralised short-term loan structured as a sale-and-repurchase of securities. Price difference = interest. Key shadow-banking funding tool.

definition: The percentage discount applied to the market value of collateral in a secured lending transaction. A 10% haircut on a €100 bond means the borrower receives only €90. Haircuts protect lenders against collateral price declines. In the GFC, haircuts on structured products rose sharply and rapidly – in Gorton & Metrick's account, this was a 'run on repo' as effectively as any bank run.
flashcardBack: Discount on collateral value in secured lending. Rising haircuts in 2007–08 functioned as a shadow-banking bank run.

definition: A bilateral derivative contract in which the protection buyer pays a periodic premium (the CDS spread, in basis points) in exchange for a contingent payment from the protection seller if a reference entity suffers a credit event (default, restructuring, failure to pay). Functions economically like insurance on a bond. AIG's near-collapse in September 2008 was directly attributable to its exposure as a protection seller on roughly $440bn of CDS referencing structured-credit products.
flashcardBack: Derivative paying protection buyer upon credit event. Buyer pays periodic spread; AIG's CDS book on MBS nearly brought down the firm in 2008.

definition: An off-balance-sheet entity sponsored by a bank that funded itself by issuing short-term asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) and medium-term notes, then invested the proceeds in longer-term, higher-yielding ABS and CDOs. The maturity mismatch was monetised as the yield spread. When ABCP markets froze in August 2007 – triggered by BNP Paribas suspending redemptions – SIVs could no longer roll their funding and sponsors faced the choice of letting them fail or absorbing them back onto the balance sheet.
flashcardBack: Off-balance-sheet vehicle funding long ABS/CDO positions with short ABCP. Maturity mismatch collapsed when ABCP markets froze in Aug 2007.

definition: An FX swap is a simultaneous spot sale and forward purchase (or vice versa) of currency. Covered Interest Parity (CIP) states that the forward premium should equal the interest-rate differential, so that borrowing in one currency and swapping into another should yield no profit. The cross-currency basis is the deviation from CIP: a negative basis (dollar basis) means it is more expensive than CIP implies to borrow dollars via FX swaps. This basis blew out sharply in 2008 and again in 2020, reflecting dollar funding stress – and central bank dollar swap lines with the Fed were the primary policy response.
flashcardBack: Cross-currency basis = deviation from Covered Interest Parity in FX swap markets. Negative dollar basis signals dollar funding stress; cured by Fed swap lines.

definition: A central bank's function of providing emergency liquidity to solvent but illiquid financial institutions. Articulated by Bagehot (1873): lend freely, at penalty rates, against good collateral. The classic LOLR prevents a liquidity crisis from becoming a solvency crisis. The distinction between illiquidity and insolvency is, in practice, extremely difficult to make in real time – the central bank cannot observe the true value of assets during a panic.
flashcardBack: Central bank provides emergency liquidity to solvent-but-illiquid banks. Bagehot: lend freely, at penalty rate, against good collateral.

definition: A resolution tool under BRRD that writes down or converts to equity the claims of a failing bank's creditors to restore capital adequacy, without recourse to taxpayer funds. The order of loss absorption follows the capital structure (equity → AT1 → T2 → senior unsecured → deposits). Bail-in replaced the pre-crisis 'bail-out' norm and is operationalised through the MREL requirement, which mandates that banks hold a minimum quantum of bail-in-able liabilities.
flashcardBack: Writes down creditor claims to recapitalise a failing bank without taxpayer funds. MREL ensures sufficient bail-in-able liabilities exist.

term: Minimum Requirement for own funds and Eligible Liabilities (MREL)
definition: A BRRD-derived requirement that sets a minimum level of loss-absorbing and recapitalisation capacity for each bank subject to resolution planning. MREL liabilities must be capable of bearing losses – i.e., they must be unsecured, have an original maturity of at least one year, and not be eligible for deposit insurance. MREL is bank-specific, calibrated by resolution authorities, and expressed as a percentage of total risk exposure or total liabilities. The US equivalent is TLAC (Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity).
flashcardBack: Bank-specific minimum of bail-in-able liabilities under BRRD. Must be unsecured, ≥1 year maturity, not deposit-insured. US equivalent: TLAC.

definition: Outside money is a claim on an entity outside the private sector – central bank reserves and banknotes are the canonical example. Inside money is a claim on a private entity: bank deposits are inside money because one person's deposit is another's liability. Inside money nets to zero across the private sector; outside money does not. The distinction matters for understanding money creation: commercial banks create inside money when they make loans, not when central banks print.
flashcardBack: Outside money: claims on central bank (reserves, notes). Inside money: private-sector claims (deposits). Inside money nets to zero; created by bank lending.

definition: A guarantee scheme, typically government-backed, that protects depositors up to a specified ceiling against loss in the event of bank failure. In the Diamond–Dybvig framework, deposit insurance eliminates the bad equilibrium (bank run) because depositors have no incentive to withdraw early if their deposits are safe regardless of what others do. The cost is moral hazard: insured depositors have weakened incentives to monitor bank risk, and insured banks have incentives to take excessive risk (since losses are partially socialised).
flashcardBack: Government guarantee on deposits up to a limit. Eliminates run equilibrium (Diamond–Dybvig) but introduces moral hazard on bank risk-taking.

definition: A fixed-income instrument backed by a pool of mortgage loans. Cash flows from principal and interest payments on the underlying mortgages are passed through (pass-through MBS) or tranched (CMO) to investors. Agency MBS (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae) carry implicit or explicit government guarantees. Non-agency (private-label) MBS pools subprime and alt-A mortgages; their AAA ratings, based on house-price assumptions that proved catastrophically wrong, were central to the GFC.
flashcardBack: Bond backed by mortgage pool. Agency MBS: government-guaranteed. Private-label subprime MBS: AAA-rated based on flawed house-price models; GFC epicentre.

definition: A structured finance product that pools credit-risky assets (bonds, loans, ABS tranches) and issues tranches of varying seniority. Senior tranches absorb losses last and were typically rated AAA; equity tranches absorb losses first. CDO-squared products pooled BBB tranches of MBS into a new CDO, creating large volumes of synthetic AAA from deeply subprime collateral. Their complexity concealed correlation risk that models systematically underestimated.
flashcardBack: Pools credit assets and issues tranches. Senior = last loss (AAA); equity = first loss. CDO-squared amplified subprime exposure with fabricated AAA ratings.

definition: A condition in which one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other. In credit markets the borrower knows more about their own repayment capacity and intentions than the lender. Asymmetric information is the root of two distinct frictions: adverse selection (pre-contract, hidden information) and moral hazard (post-contract, hidden action). Banks exist in part to economise on the costs of mitigating both.
flashcardBack: One party knows more than the other. Generates adverse selection (pre-contract) and moral hazard (post-contract). Foundational reason banks exist.

definition: A pre-contract (ex-ante) information problem in which the lender cannot distinguish high-risk from low-risk borrowers. With pooled pricing, low-risk borrowers find the offered rate too high and exit, leaving the pool dominated by high-risk borrowers – the lemons problem. Stiglitz–Weiss show this can produce equilibrium credit rationing: raising rates worsens the pool, so banks ration quantity rather than clear the market on price.
flashcardBack: Pre-contract hidden-information problem. Lemons drive quality out of the pool. Drives credit rationing under Stiglitz–Weiss.

definition: A post-contract (ex-post) information problem in which a party takes more risk than they otherwise would because they do not bear the full downside. Examples: a borrower diverts loan proceeds to a riskier project after disbursement; an insured bank takes excessive risk because losses are partly socialised; an AT1 holder under-monitors because the bank knows write-down requires regulatory action. Mitigated by monitoring, covenants, collateral, and skin-in-the-game requirements.
flashcardBack: Post-contract hidden-action problem. Protected party takes more risk because downside is borne by others. Mitigated by monitoring, covenants, collateral.

definition: Seminal asymmetric-information model. Buyers cannot observe quality, so they price at the average; high-quality sellers exit; the pool worsens; in extremis the market unravels and only lemons trade. Solutions include warranties (non-dissipative signal), reputation, certification, and guarantees. Examined numerically on past finals (e.g. Final 2022 Q2 with three quality types).
flashcardBack: Asymmetric-info model: buyers price-down → high-quality exits → only lemons remain. Solutions: warranties, reputation, certification.

definition: Bank's expected return is non-monotonic in the loan rate r. Raising r above r* worsens the pool (adverse selection – safe borrowers drop out) and incentivises risky projects (moral hazard – only those who don't expect to repay accept the rate). Beyond r*, expected profit falls. Banks therefore ration the quantity of credit at r* rather than clearing the market on price. Equilibrium credit rationing emerges from informational frictions, not regulation.
flashcardBack: Bank expected return is non-monotonic in r. Above r*, pool worsens and risk rises. Banks ration quantity, not price. Equilibrium credit rationing from info frictions.

definition: Equilibrium denial of credit to some borrowers at the profit-maximising loan rate, despite their willingness to pay more. Distinct from market clearing on price. Arises in Stiglitz–Weiss because raising rates further triggers adverse selection and moral hazard, lowering expected returns. Means credit markets do not 'clear' in the Walrasian sense, and a credit crunch can persist even at high rates.
flashcardBack: Quantity-rationing of credit at the profit-max rate r*. Higher rates would worsen pool quality and incentives. Stiglitz–Weiss equilibrium.

definition: Banks act as agents for many small savers, monitoring borrowers on their behalf. Without the bank, each saver would have to monitor each borrower at duplicated cost; with the bank, monitoring scales and diversification across loans makes the bank's promise to depositors credible. Diamond's model formalises why the bank intermediary dominates direct lending in the presence of monitoring costs and asymmetric information.
flashcardBack: Banks monitor borrowers on behalf of many small savers. Economies of scale + diversification make monitoring credible. Justifies the bank as intermediary.

definition: Screening is ex-ante effort to identify borrower quality before lending – credit scoring, financial-statement analysis, due diligence. It mitigates adverse selection. Monitoring is ex-post effort to observe borrower behaviour after lending – covenant tracking, periodic reporting, site visits. It mitigates moral hazard. The two are sequential responses to the two distinct information frictions and constitute the core of bank lending technology.
flashcardBack: Screening = ex-ante (mitigates AS). Monitoring = ex-post (mitigates MH). Sequential responses to the two informational frictions.

definition: Contractual restrictions on borrower behaviour to mitigate moral hazard. Six standard classes: (1) Affirmative – must do (deliver financial statements, maintain insurance); (2) Negative – must not do (extra debt, asset sales, dividends without consent); (3) Financial – maintain ratios (debt/equity, ICR, leverage); (4) Operational – restrict business activities; (5) Reporting – deliver specified data on schedule; (6) Event of Default – defines triggers (non-payment, cross-default, insolvency). Feb 2025 mid-term Q1 was 30 points on covenants.
flashcardBack: Six classes: Affirmative, Negative, Financial, Operational, Reporting, Event of Default. Mitigate moral hazard by restricting borrower behaviour.

definition: Lender's election not to enforce its remedies after a covenant breach. Reasons include: breach is minor or temporary, the borrower is fundamentally viable, enforcement would crystallise larger losses than continued forbearance, the bank values the relationship, or waiver is a prelude to renegotiation on amended terms. Granting a waiver does not remove the breach from the record and may be conditional on remedial action.
flashcardBack: Lender's choice not to enforce after covenant breach. Granted to preserve relationship, avoid larger losses, or set up renegotiation. Often conditional.

term: Collateral as Signal (mitigates BOTH AS and MH)
definition: Collateral pledges play a dual role. (1) Adverse selection: high-risk borrowers are less willing to pledge collateral because they expect to lose it; pledging therefore signals borrower confidence and quality. (2) Moral hazard: pledged collateral creates 'skin in the game' – the borrower has more to lose from the risky project, restoring incentive alignment. Collateral is the canonical mitigant that addresses both informational frictions simultaneously.
flashcardBack: Collateral mitigates BOTH adverse selection (signal of borrower confidence) AND moral hazard (skin in the game).

definition: When informed parties can take observable actions correlated with hidden quality, they can signal and produce a separating equilibrium in which types are revealed. A signal works only if the Incentive-Compatibility (IC) constraint binds: low types must find mimicking the high-type signal more costly than truthful behaviour. Akerlof's warranty is the textbook example: high-quality sellers offer it cheaply, low-quality cannot afford to.
flashcardBack: Observable action correlated with quality reveals types if the IC constraint binds – low types must find mimicking too costly. Yields a separating equilibrium.

definition: A non-dissipative signal preserves total surplus – e.g., a costless warranty that only the high-quality seller can credibly offer because they expect not to pay it out. A dissipative signal destroys surplus – e.g., expensive education in Spence's job-market model, which has no productive value but reveals type. Bank disclosure and capital ratios sit between the two: informative but with real compliance cost.
flashcardBack: Non-dissipative signal preserves surplus (warranty). Dissipative signal destroys it (costly education). Both reveal type if IC binds.

definition: Foundational model of bank runs and the role of demand deposits. Banks fund illiquid long-duration projects with demandable deposits and provide liquidity insurance to risk-averse depositors with random consumption needs. The structure produces two equilibria: a good equilibrium in which only those with genuine liquidity needs withdraw, and a bad equilibrium – a self-fulfilling run – in which everyone withdraws because everyone expects everyone else to. Three solutions eliminate the bad equilibrium: deposit insurance, lender of last resort, and suspension of convertibility. Cited on every recent GRA6546 paper.
flashcardBack: Two-equilibrium model. Demand deposits = liquidity insurance. Bad equilibrium = self-fulfilling run. Cured by deposit insurance, LOLR, or suspension of convertibility.

definition: A bank's refusal – typically temporary and statutory – to honour withdrawal requests above a certain threshold. In Diamond–Dybvig it is one of three solutions to the bad-equilibrium run, alongside deposit insurance and LOLR. Suspension stops the panic by removing the strategic incentive to withdraw early. Practical drawbacks: it harms depositors with genuine liquidity needs and damages the bank's reputation. Used historically (US 1907, 1933) but largely supplanted by deposit insurance.
flashcardBack: Bank temporarily refuses to honour withdrawals beyond a threshold. One of three D-D run cures. Harms genuine-need depositors; rare today after deposit insurance.

triage_reason: Marcus 1984 / S&L crisis – tested in DI / Norway crisis context
definition: The present value of future economic rents accruing to a bank from its operating franchise – relationship capital, regulatory protection from entry, payments-system access. Insolvency forfeits the charter, so banks with high charter value have endogenous incentives to limit risk-taking even with deposit insurance. Marcus's 1984 framework explains why deregulating the US thrift industry in the early 1980s – which compressed charter values – is widely seen as a cause of the S&L crisis.
flashcardBack: PV of franchise rents. Insolvency forfeits the charter, deterring excessive risk. Compressed charter values explain S&L deregulation crisis (Marcus 1984).

definition: Two distinct intermediation models. Brokerage matches savers to borrowers without taking the assets onto the intermediary's balance sheet – securities firms, peer-to-peer platforms, or pure advisory. The intermediary bears no credit, liquidity, or interest-rate risk. Qualitative Asset Transformation (banks) holds claims on its own balance sheet that differ from its liabilities along multiple dimensions; the intermediary bears the resulting risks and earns the spread. Banks' regulatory burden derives from QAT, not brokerage.
flashcardBack: Brokerage = matchmaking, no balance-sheet risk. QAT = mismatched balance sheet, intermediary bears risk and earns spread. Banks' regulation flows from QAT.

term: Net Interest Income (NII) & Net Interest Margin (NIM)
definition: NII = interest income on assets minus interest expense on liabilities; the primary revenue line of a traditional bank. NIM = NII / average earning assets, expressed as a percentage. Typical NIM in developed-market banks is 0.5–2%. NIM compresses when the yield curve flattens or when funding costs rise faster than asset yields. Mid-term 2024 P1Q2 required a numerical NIM calculation.
flashcardBack: NII = interest income − interest expense. NIM = NII / avg earning assets, ~0.5–2%. Core revenue measure for traditional banks.

definition: ROA = net income / total assets; ROE = net income / equity; Equity Multiplier = total assets / equity (≈ leverage). DuPont decomposition: ROE = ROA × Equity Multiplier. A bank can achieve low single-digit ROA but double-digit ROE because the multiplier is typically 10–20×. The crisis-era investment banks ran multipliers of 30–50×. The decomposition makes explicit that bank profitability is largely a leverage story.
flashcardBack: ROE = ROA × Equity Multiplier. Banks: low ROA × high leverage = double-digit ROE. Pre-crisis IBs ran 30–50× multipliers.

definition: Operating expenses divided by operating income (NII + fees + trading). A standard efficiency metric for banks. Below ~50% is considered efficient; Nordic banks typically operate at 40–50%. Tested numerically on Final 2022 Q4. C/I rises in cost-heavy retail networks and falls in scaled, technology-driven banks.
flashcardBack: Operating expenses / operating income. <50% is efficient. Nordic banks ~40–50%. Tested numerically Final 2022 Q4.

definition: Loan-to-Deposit (LDR) = total loans / total deposits; Deposit-to-Loan is the inverse. Measures funding self-sufficiency: a ratio of 100% means deposits fund all lending. Above 100% indicates wholesale-funding reliance – a fragility flagged in SVB and Northern Rock. Tested numerically on Mid-term 2024 Q1 and Final 2023 Q5.
flashcardBack: LDR = loans / deposits. >100% → wholesale-funding reliance, a fragility signal. Tested on Mid-term 2024 Q1, Final 2023 Q5.

definition: Loans more than 90 days past due or otherwise unlikely to be repaid in full – broadly equivalent to IFRS 9 Stage 3. NPL ratio = NPLs / total loans. Nordic banks run NPL ratios below 1%; Southern European banks reached 15%+ in the eurozone crisis. NPLs trigger lifetime ECL provisioning and consume capital via specific impairment.
flashcardBack: Loans >90 days past due or unlikely-to-pay (≈ IFRS 9 Stage 3). Nordic banks <1%, eurozone-crisis peripheries hit 15%+.

definition: International accounting standard for financial-instrument classification, measurement, and impairment, in force from 2018. Replaced IAS 39. Two key innovations: (1) classification driven by business-model and SPPI tests, mapping instruments to amortised cost, FVOCI, or FVTPL; (2) forward-looking Expected Credit Loss (ECL) impairment, replacing the incurred-loss model. Tested directly on every recent GRA6546 paper.
flashcardBack: Accounting standard from 2018 replacing IAS 39. Adds business-model classification (AC/FVOCI/FVTPL) and forward-looking ECL impairment.

definition: IFRS 9's forward-looking impairment metric. Computed as EAD × PD × LGD over either a 12-month horizon (Stage 1) or the remaining lifetime of the exposure (Stages 2 and 3). Probability-weighted across multiple macroeconomic scenarios. Replaced IAS 39's incurred-loss model because the latter delayed loss recognition into a downturn, amplifying procyclicality.
flashcardBack: ECL = EAD × PD × LGD. 12-month (Stage 1) or lifetime (Stage 2/3). Probability-weighted across scenarios. Replaced IAS 39 incurred-loss.

definition: Impairment-staging machinery. Stage 1: performing loans; provision = 12-month ECL; interest accrued on gross carrying amount. Stage 2: loans showing a Significant Increase in Credit Risk (SICR) since origination but not yet credit-impaired; provision = lifetime ECL; interest still on gross. Stage 3: credit-impaired (≈ NPL); provision = lifetime ECL; interest accrued on net carrying amount. Movement is bidirectional, but cure rules from Stage 3 are conservative.
flashcardBack: Stage 1: performing, 12-mo ECL, gross interest. Stage 2: SICR, lifetime ECL, gross interest. Stage 3: credit-impaired, lifetime ECL, net interest.

definition: IFRS 9 trigger that moves an exposure from Stage 1 to Stage 2, switching provisioning from 12-month to lifetime ECL. Driven by changes in PD since origination, supported by qualitative indicators (watchlist, forbearance, payment behaviour). Crucially, deterioration in collateral value alone does NOT trigger SICR – a recurring T/F trap, tested explicitly on Feb 2025 Q4(e).
flashcardBack: Trigger from Stage 1 → 2 driven by changes in PD since origination. Collateral deterioration alone does NOT trigger SICR – Feb 2025 Q4(e) trap.

definition: Pre-IFRS 9 international accounting standard for financial instruments. Used an 'incurred-loss' impairment model: provisions only when objective evidence of loss had been observed. Criticised after the GFC because losses were recognised too late, amplifying procyclicality – banks looked healthy on the way down and recognised losses only when the downturn was already advanced. Replaced by IFRS 9's forward-looking ECL in 2018.
flashcardBack: Pre-2018 standard. Incurred-loss model: provision only after objective evidence. Procyclical – recognised losses too late. Replaced by IFRS 9 ECL.

definition: IFRS 9 classification – formally Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income – for debt instruments held under a 'hold-to-collect-and-sell' business model. Carried at fair value on the balance sheet; unrealised gains and losses bypass the P&L and accumulate in OCI within equity. Realised on disposal. AFS bonds therefore mark to market in book equity but not in reported earnings – a key distinction from FVTPL.
flashcardBack: Fair value on B/S, but unrealised gains/losses go to OCI (equity), not P&L. 'Hold-to-collect-and-sell' business model.

definition: IFRS 9 classification for debt instruments held under a 'hold-to-collect' business model with SPPI cash flows. Carried at amortised cost; fair-value changes are not recognised on the balance sheet or in P&L – only disclosed in notes. The SVB collapse in March 2023 was driven by a $115bn HTM portfolio of long-duration Treasuries with large unrealised losses that became real once SVB had to sell to meet deposit outflows.
flashcardBack: Amortised-cost accounting. 'Hold-to-collect', SPPI. Fair-value losses hidden until sale. SVB's HTM Treasuries crystallised on forced sale, March 2023.

definition: IFRS 9 classification of last resort: instruments not meeting the SPPI test or held in trading book. Carried at fair value on the balance sheet, with all changes – realised and unrealised – flowing through the P&L. Maximum earnings volatility. Default classification for derivatives, equity investments, and structured products with embedded leverage.
flashcardBack: Mark-to-market through P&L. Maximum earnings volatility. Derivatives, equities, complex/leveraged instruments default here.

triage_reason: sub-acronym of FVOCI – your example for drop
definition: Equity-account bucket capturing unrealised gains and losses that bypass the P&L. Includes AFS/FVOCI revaluation, cash-flow hedge effective portion, and pension actuarial gains/losses. Released to P&L on realisation (recycling) for some items, never for others (own-credit on FVTPL liabilities). OCI is why a bank can have negative tangible equity revaluation without reporting any loss in net income.
flashcardBack: Equity bucket for unrealised gains/losses (AFS/FVOCI revaluation, cash-flow hedges). Some items recycle to P&L on realisation, others never.

definition: Accounting basis for HTM/hold-to-collect debt instruments under IFRS 9. Carrying value = original cost adjusted for principal repayments and accumulated amortisation of any discount/premium using the effective-interest method, less any impairment. Fair-value movements are not reflected. Primary location for a bank's loan book and HTM bond portfolio.
flashcardBack: Cost ± principal/EIR amortisation − impairment. Used for HTM/hold-to-collect. Fair-value movements ignored. Loan book and HTM bonds.

definition: Cumulative stock of provisions netted against gross loans on the asset side of the balance sheet. A counter-asset. Increased by impairment charges through the P&L; decreased by write-offs (and recoveries reverse them). Net loans = gross loans − LLR. Mid-term 2024 P1Q5 required reconciling opening LLR + new charges − write-offs = closing LLR.
flashcardBack: Stock of provisions netted from gross loans. Counter-asset. ΔLLR = new charges − write-offs. Mid-term 2024 P1Q5 reconciliation.

term: Impairment Charge / Provision for Loan Loss
definition: P&L expense recognising the period's increase in expected credit losses. Flows through net income and reduces capital, while simultaneously increasing the LLR counter-asset on the balance sheet. Under IFRS 9 the charge is forward-looking (ECL); under IAS 39 it required objective evidence of incurred loss. The charge is one of the largest discretionary items in a bank's P&L.
flashcardBack: P&L expense increasing LLR; reduces net income and capital. IFRS 9: forward-looking ECL. Largest discretionary P&L line.

definition: Removal of a loan from the balance sheet when the bank has no reasonable expectation of recovery. The gross loan is reduced and the corresponding LLR is consumed; net P&L impact is zero (the loss was already provisioned). Subsequent recoveries flow back through the P&L. Distinct from default – a loan can be in default for years before being written off.
flashcardBack: Removes loan + corresponding LLR. No P&L impact (already provisioned). Distinct from default. Recoveries flow back through P&L.

definition: Gross loans = principal amount owed by borrowers. Net loans = gross loans − accumulated impairment (LLR). The difference is the cumulative ECL provision. Reported balance-sheet loans are typically net; gross figures appear in note disclosures. Mid-term 2024 Q4 directly tested the distinction.
flashcardBack: Gross = principal owed. Net = gross − accumulated impairment. Reported figure usually net. Mid-term 2024 Q4 tested directly.

definition: Period-over-period change in book equity equals retained earnings of the period: net profit minus dividends paid (plus capital issued, minus buybacks). Mid-term 2024 P1Q3 required this reconciliation directly. The identity is the link between income-statement profitability and balance-sheet capital – and the mechanism by which dividends erode regulatory capital.
flashcardBack: ΔEquity = Profit − Dividends (± issuance/buybacks). Links P&L to balance-sheet capital. Mid-term 2024 P1Q3.

definition: Period change in the loan-loss reserve equals impairment charges through the P&L minus loans written off (plus recoveries). Closing LLR = opening LLR + new charges − write-offs + recoveries. Mid-term 2024 P1Q5 required this reconciliation; it is the standard mechanical question on bank impairment accounting.
flashcardBack: ΔLLR = new impairment charges − write-offs + recoveries. Mid-term 2024 P1Q5 mechanical.

triage_reason: OBS items list – useful context; specific clauses are sub-detail
term: Off-Balance-Sheet Items (Loan Commitments, SBLC, BA, MAC)
definition: Contingent claims that do not appear on the on-balance-sheet asset/liability totals but generate exposure. Loan commitments (committed credit lines, including kassekreditt); Standby Letters of Credit (SBLC) – bank's promise to pay if borrower defaults on third party; Commercial Letters of Credit and Banker's Acceptances (remburs) – trade-finance instruments; Material Adverse Change (MAC) clauses – let the bank withdraw a commitment if borrower's circumstances deteriorate. All consume capital via Credit Conversion Factors and feed into RWA.
flashcardBack: Contingent exposures: loan commitments, SBLC, L/Cs, banker's acceptances, MAC clauses. CCF-converted into RWA. Off-B/S but capital-consuming.

definition: Banks fund long-duration assets (mortgages, business loans) with short-duration liabilities (sight deposits, money-market funding) and earn the term premium. One of the five QAT dimensions. Generates liquidity creation for the economy but exposes the bank to roll-over risk and interest-rate risk. Mid-term 2024 P2d directly tested the concept as a T/F.
flashcardBack: Long-duration assets funded with short-duration liabilities. Earns term premium. Source of liquidity creation AND roll-over/IR risk. Mid-term 2024 P2d.

definition: System in which banks hold only a fraction of deposit liabilities as central-bank reserves and lend out the remainder. Relies on most depositors not withdrawing simultaneously. The textbook story is that this multiplies central-bank reserves into a larger money supply via the deposit multiplier; the modern view (BoE 2014) is that banks create deposits when they lend, and reserves accommodate ex post. Spring 2024 Q2c+d tested the concept directly.
flashcardBack: Banks hold a fraction of deposits as reserves; lend the rest. Textbook: reserves → money via multiplier. Modern view: lending creates deposits, reserves follow. Spring 2024 Q2c+d.

triage_reason: BoE 2014 says it is the wrong model – useful as foil
definition: Textbook formula: a unit increase in central-bank reserves expands deposits by 1/r, where r is the reserve ratio. Implies money supply = central-bank reserves × multiplier. Course lectures emphasise that this is the wrong-way-round causal story for modern banks: reserves do not constrain lending in the short run. Likely T/F trap on the exam.
flashcardBack: Textbook: ΔDeposits = ΔReserves / r. Lectures stress this is causally backwards in modern banks – loans create deposits, not the reverse. T/F trap.

term: Money Creation in the Modern Economy ('Loans Create Deposits', BoE 2014)
definition: Bank of England 2014 paper articulating the modern view: when a commercial bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a deposit on the borrower's account – both sides of the bank's balance sheet expand. Reserves are not the constraint; capital and risk appetite are. Central-bank reserves accommodate banks' reserve demand ex post via repo operations or QE. Reframes the textbook fractional-reserve / money-multiplier story.
flashcardBack: BoE 2014: loans create deposits – both sides of bank B/S expand. Reserves accommodate ex post; capital is the binding constraint. Reframes textbook multiplier.

definition: Central-bank purchases of long-dated government bonds (and sometimes corporate bonds, MBS) financed by creating reserves. Expands central-bank balance sheet and floods the banking system with reserves. Effects: lowers term premia, supports asset prices, supplies liquidity in stress. QE expands inside money only if banks lend the new reserves; absent that, broad money grows little. Reversal is QT.
flashcardBack: CB buys long-duration assets, paying with new reserves. Lowers term premia, supports asset prices. Broad money expands only if banks lend the reserves.

definition: Historical illustration of fractional-reserve emergence. Goldsmiths warehoused depositors' gold and issued warehouse receipts. When goldsmiths realised that receipts were used as money and that not all depositors withdrew simultaneously, they began lending out gold and issuing additional receipts beyond gold reserves. This created inside money and the original maturity-transformation business – and the original bank-run risk.
flashcardBack: Goldsmiths issued more warehouse receipts than gold held – first fractional reserve. Created inside money and the first run risk.

definition: Money markets trade short-term debt instruments with original maturity of 12 months or less (T-bills, commercial paper, interbank loans, repos). Capital markets trade longer-dated debt and equity. The distinction is purely about maturity, NOT about liquidity – a recurring T/F trap. Some money-market instruments are illiquid in stress (ABCP in 2007); some long-dated instruments are highly liquid (US Treasuries). Mid-term 2024 P2c tested this directly.
flashcardBack: Maturity distinction (≤12mo vs >12mo), NOT liquidity. T/F trap: money-market ≠ liquid (ABCP froze 2007). Mid-term 2024 P2c.

term: Commercial Paper vs Interbank Lending vs Repo
definition: Three short-term funding markets. Commercial paper: unsecured corporate/bank promissory notes, typically 1–270 days, sold at discount. Interbank: unsecured wholesale lending between banks (NIBOR/EURIBOR/SOFR fixings derive from this). Repo: secured against collateral, with a haircut; the survivor of 2007–08 because secured. The crisis migration was unsecured → secured → central-bank balance sheets. Spring 2024 Q2e tested the typology.
flashcardBack: CP: unsecured short-term notes. Interbank: unsecured bank-to-bank. Repo: secured with haircut. Crisis migrated unsecured → secured → CB. Spring 2024 Q2e.

triage_reason: modern systems do not bind on reserves – context
definition: Mandatory minimum balances banks must hold at the central bank as a fraction of certain deposit liabilities. Two functions discussed in lectures: (1) liquidity backstop preventing banks from offloading their liquidity-management problem onto the LOLR; (2) seigniorage capture – non-remunerated reserves act as an implicit tax on banks, sharing seigniorage between the state and the banking system. Now largely supplemented by LCR/NSFR.
flashcardBack: Min reserves at CB. Functions: (1) liquidity backstop, (2) implicit tax sharing seigniorage. Largely supplemented by LCR/NSFR today.

definition: Pre-contractual document summarising the principal commercial terms of a proposed loan: amount, currency, tenor, pricing (margin over benchmark), security, covenants, conditions precedent, repayment schedule. Usually non-binding except for confidentiality and exclusivity clauses. Used to align bank and borrower before formal documentation drafting. Featured on the GRA6546 reading list.
flashcardBack: Pre-contract summary of loan commercial terms (amount, tenor, price, security, covenants). Mostly non-binding. Anchor for documentation drafting.

definition: Regulatory due-diligence requirements applied during loan origination and account opening. KYC verifies customer identity, beneficial ownership, and risk profile. AML monitors transactions for suspicious patterns, with mandatory reporting (e.g. Norwegian FIU). Failure carries large fines (DNB was fined NOK 400m in 2021 for AML breaches). Embedded in the conditions-precedent step of loan disbursement.
flashcardBack: Origination due diligence: identity (KYC), transaction monitoring (AML). Mandatory FIU reporting. Large penalties – DNB NOK 400m in 2021.

triage_reason: sub-clauses of CP / MAC – your example for drop
definition: Borrower obligations that must be satisfied before a loan can be disbursed. Standard CPs: signed loan agreement, KYC/AML verification, security perfection, legal opinions, certified financial statements, insurance, no material adverse change. Until all CPs are met, the bank's commitment is contingent and the loan does not draw. CPs are the bank's last line of defence before money goes out the door.
flashcardBack: Borrower obligations to satisfy before disbursement: KYC, security perfection, legal opinions, no MAC. Last defence before money leaves.

definition: Drawdown: the act of borrowing under a committed facility, transferring funds from commitment to outstanding loan. Take-down schedule: the agreed timing of drawdowns. Balloon payment: a single large repayment at maturity, typical of bullet loans where most of the principal is not amortised. Feb 2025 Q4d tested 'balloon' as a direct T/F.
flashcardBack: Drawdown = borrowing under a commitment. Balloon = lump-sum repayment at maturity. Feb 2025 Q4d direct T/F.

term: Loan Facility Taxonomy (Term Loan, Revolving, Line of Credit, Kassekreditt, Working Capital)
definition: Term loan: fixed amount drawn at closing, amortised on a schedule, no re-borrow. Revolving credit facility (RCF): borrower can draw, repay, and re-draw up to a limit during the availability period. Line of credit / kassekreditt (Norwegian): overdraft-style RCF tied to a current account, used for working-capital fluctuations. Working-capital loan: short-term, often secured against receivables/inventory. Each carries different commitment fees, RWA treatment, and covenant packages.
flashcardBack: Term loan: drawn once, amortised. RCF: revolves up to a limit. Kassekreditt: overdraft-style line. Working-capital: short, against receivables. Different commitment fees and RWA.

definition: Likelihood that a borrower defaults within a specified horizon, typically one year. Estimated from internal scoring models (IRB), external ratings (Standardised), or market prices (CDS-implied). Combined with LGD and EAD to produce expected loss. Under IFRS 9, changes in PD since origination drive SICR and Stage 1 → 2 migration. The single most important credit-risk parameter.
flashcardBack: 1-year default probability. From IRB internal models, external ratings, or CDS-implied. Drives SICR under IFRS 9. Most important credit parameter.

definition: Fraction of exposure not recovered after default. LGD = 1 − Recovery Rate. Driven by collateral coverage, lien priority, jurisdiction-specific recovery processes, and economic conditions at default (downturn LGD is regulator-mandated for IRB). Typical secured retail mortgage LGDs run 10–30%; senior unsecured corporate LGDs 40–60%; subordinated and equity 80–100%.
flashcardBack: 1 − Recovery Rate. Driven by collateral, seniority, jurisdiction. Secured mortgage 10–30%, senior unsecured 40–60%, subordinated 80–100%.

definition: Amount the borrower owes the bank at the moment of default. For drawn loans, equals outstanding principal plus accrued interest. For commitments and revolving facilities, includes expected drawdown of currently undrawn limits – modelled via a Credit Conversion Factor (CCF) on the unused line. Important: EAD is forward-looking, capturing borrower behaviour as conditions deteriorate.
flashcardBack: Owed amount at default = drawn + expected drawdown of undrawn (via CCF). Forward-looking, captures behaviour as borrower deteriorates.

triage_reason: M parameter – sub-detail of IRB formula
definition: Fourth IRB capital-formula parameter: the effective remaining maturity of the exposure, capped at five years. Longer maturities attract higher capital because of greater migration risk over the horizon. Under IRB Foundation, regulators set M (typically 2.5y for corporates); under IRB Advanced, banks estimate it from contractual cash flows.
flashcardBack: Effective remaining maturity (capped at 5y) in IRB capital formula. Longer M → more capital. Reg-set in IRB-F (2.5y default), bank-set in IRB-A.

term: Basel Credit-Risk Approaches: Standardised vs IRB-F vs IRB-A
definition: Three regulatory approaches to credit-risk RWA. Standardised: regulator-prescribed risk weights, typically based on external ratings or asset class (e.g. 100% on unrated corporate, 35% on residential mortgages). IRB Foundation: bank estimates PD; regulator supplies LGD, EAD, M. IRB Advanced: bank estimates all four parameters. IRB requires supervisory model approval and continuous validation; Basel III introduced output floors limiting RWA savings vs the Standardised approach.
flashcardBack: Standardised: regulator-set weights. IRB-F: bank PD, regulator LGD/EAD/M. IRB-A: bank estimates all four. Basel III adds output floor vs Standardised.

triage_reason: IRB regulatory K formula – not tested numerically
definition: Capital requirement K per unit of EAD = LGD × [N((G(PD) + √R · G(0.999)) / √(1−R)) − PD] × maturity adjustment. The bracketed term is the conditional default probability at the 99.9% one-year stress (the worst-case point from a single systematic factor with asset correlation R). The formula sizes capital to cover Unexpected Loss only; Expected Loss is covered by IFRS 9 provisions. Conceptual exam question; numerical calculation rare.
flashcardBack: K = LGD × [N((G(PD) + √R · G(0.999))/√(1−R)) − PD] × M-adj. Sized for UL at 99.9% one-year. EL covered by provisions. Asset correlation R from regulator.

definition: The tail loss in excess of expected loss, measured at a high confidence level – Basel uses 99.9% over a one-year horizon. Capital is sized to absorb UL; provisions (ECL) are sized to absorb EL. The split is the regulatory backbone: provisions deplete in the central case, capital absorbs the tail. Conflating UL and EL is a common exam error.
flashcardBack: Tail loss above EL, at 99.9% / 1-year. Covered by capital. EL covered by provisions. Split is regulatory backbone – common exam confusion.

definition: Tendency of financial-sector behaviour and regulation to amplify the business cycle. In booms, asset prices rise, risk weights fall, capital ratios appear strong, lending expands. In busts, the opposite squeeze occurs precisely when the economy needs credit. The Turner Review identified procyclicality as one of the six causes of the GFC; CCyB and IFRS 9 ECL were designed in part to counter it.
flashcardBack: Regulation/behaviour amplifying cycle: capital looks strong in boom, squeezed in bust. Turner cause; CCyB and IFRS 9 ECL designed to counter.

definition: Risk-measurement metric: the loss threshold not exceeded with a given probability over a specified horizon (e.g. 99% one-day VaR of $50m means 1% chance of losing more than $50m in a day). Pre-crisis foundation of trading-book capital. Criticised post-crisis for ignoring tail risk beyond the threshold (a 1-in-1000 day's loss can be much larger), assuming normality, and producing pro-cyclical capital. Replaced for trading book by Expected Shortfall under FRTB.
flashcardBack: Loss threshold at given probability/horizon. Pre-crisis trading-book backbone. Failed because ignored fat tails, assumed normality. Replaced by ES under FRTB.

definition: Frank Knight's 1921 distinction: risk is measurable (probabilities can be assigned), uncertainty is not (the underlying distribution is unknown or unknowable). Cited in the Turner Review as a structural failure mode of pre-crisis risk management – banks treated unknowable structured-credit correlations as knowable parameters. Important conceptual T/F territory.
flashcardBack: Risk = measurable; uncertainty = unmeasurable distribution. Turner cites as structural failure: banks parameterised the unknowable.

definition: Highest-quality regulatory capital under Basel III: paid-in ordinary shares plus retained earnings, less prescribed deductions (goodwill, intangibles, deferred tax assets, certain investments in financial entities, proposed dividends). Absorbs losses on a going-concern basis. Basel III minimum: 4.5% of RWA; with the conservation buffer, 7%; with full Norwegian buffer stack for DNB, ~17%. Calculated on every recent final.
flashcardBack: Highest-quality capital: ordinary shares + retained earnings − deductions. Basel min 4.5% RWA. Going-concern loss absorption. On every recent final.

definition: Hybrid capital ranking between CET1 and Tier 2. Perpetual maturity, fully discretionary non-cumulative coupons, contractual write-down or conversion to equity if CET1 falls below a trigger (typically 5.125% or 7%). Going-concern loss absorption: takes losses while the bank still operates. Credit Suisse's CHF 16bn AT1 was written down to zero on 19 March 2023 while equity holders received UBS shares – the NCWO controversy of the resolution era.
flashcardBack: Perpetual hybrid, discretionary coupons, write-down/convert at CET1 trigger. Going-concern. Credit Suisse AT1 zeroed before equity in March 2023 → NCWO case.

definition: Subordinated, dated debt instruments (typically 10y bullet, with no incentive to redeem in the last 5y of life) ranking below senior unsecured but above AT1 and CET1 in liquidation. Absorbs losses on a gone-concern basis: written down or converted only at point of non-viability or in resolution. Eligible if remaining maturity ≥ 5 years (amortised over the last 5y). Cheaper than AT1 because gone-concern.
flashcardBack: Dated subordinated debt, ≥5y eligible (amortised in last 5y). Gone-concern loss absorption – only written down at PONV/resolution. Cheaper than AT1.

term: Risk-Weighted Assets / Risk Exposure Amount (RWA / REA)
definition: Sum across exposures of EAD × prescribed or estimated risk weight. EU prudential regulations call this 'Risk Exposure Amount (REA)'; rest of the world calls it 'RWA'. Identical concept. Denominator of every capital ratio: CET1 ratio = CET1 / RWA. RWA is computed under Standardised, IRB-F, or IRB-A approaches. Calculated on May 2025 Q6, Final 2022 Q4.
flashcardBack: Σ EAD × risk weight. EU = REA, rest = RWA. Denominator of every capital ratio. Standardised / IRB-F / IRB-A. May 2025 Q6, Final 2022 Q4.

term: Basel Pillars 1, 2 (P2R/P2G) and the supervisory architecture
definition: Three-pillar architecture from Basel II/III. Pillar 1: harmonised quantitative minima – 8% total capital + LCR + NSFR + leverage ratio. Pillar 2: supervisor's bank-specific add-ons after the SREP review. Pillar 2 Requirement (P2R) is binding and additional to P1, capturing risks under-covered by P1 (concentration, IRRBB). Pillar 2 Guidance (P2G) is non-binding supervisory expectation above P2R, intended to be used in stress. Tested verbatim on most recent papers.
flashcardBack: P1: harmonised minima (8% + LCR + NSFR + LR). P2R: binding bank-specific add-on after SREP. P2G: non-binding stress buffer above P2R.

definition: Basel II/III pillar requiring banks to disclose risk, capital, and governance information so that market participants – depositors, bondholders, equity holders – can price risk and discipline excessive risk-taking. Implemented via the EU Pillar 3 Disclosure Templates. Premise: imperfect because retail depositors don't read disclosures, but professional creditors and equity analysts do.
flashcardBack: Disclosure pillar: market discipline via standardised risk/capital reporting. Works for sophisticated creditors; weak for retail depositors.

definition: Permanent 2.5% CET1 buffer sitting above Pillar 1 minimums. If breached, the bank does not fail but faces automatic restrictions on dividends, AT1 coupons, and discretionary bonuses – the Maximum Distributable Amount (MDA) regime. The buffer is intended to be drawable in stress so banks can keep lending without breaching minima.
flashcardBack: Permanent 2.5% CET1 buffer. Breach triggers MDA – restricts dividends, AT1 coupons, bonuses. Designed to be drawn in stress.

definition: CET1 buffer between 0% and 2.5% (higher in some jurisdictions), set quarterly by national authorities to vary with the credit cycle: built up in booms when credit-to-GDP runs hot, released in busts to support lending. Norway has run CCyB at 2.5% in recent years. Direct policy response to the Turner Review's procyclicality cause.
flashcardBack: 0–2.5% CET1, set quarterly. Built up in booms, released in busts. Anti-procyclical. Norway 2.5% recently.

definition: CET1 buffer addressing structural (long-term, non-cyclical) systemic risks specific to a country, region, or sector. In Norway: 4.5% on Norwegian exposures. Distinct from CCyB (cyclical) and O-SII/G-SIB (institution-specific). Used in Nordic countries to capture concentrated exposure to commercial real estate, household leverage, and oil/shipping cycles.
flashcardBack: Structural CET1 buffer for country/sector systemic risks. Norway 4.5% on Norwegian exposures. Distinct from CCyB (cyclical) and O-SII (institution-specific).

definition: CET1 add-on for banks deemed systemically important at national level (as opposed to globally). Calibrated by national authority based on size, interconnectedness, complexity, substitutability. DNB carries an O-SII buffer of 2% in Norway. Sits above conservation, CCyB, and SyRB buffers.
flashcardBack: National-systemic CET1 add-on. DNB: 2%. Calibrated on size, interconnectedness, complexity, substitutability.

definition: CET1 buffer for Globally Systemically Important Banks designated annually by the Financial Stability Board. Five buckets ranging 1.0–3.5% based on size, interconnectedness, complexity, cross-jurisdictional activity, and substitutability. About 30 G-SIBs globally. Higher of G-SIB / O-SII applies (no double-counting).
flashcardBack: FSB-designated G-SIB CET1 add-on, 1.0–3.5% across five buckets. ~30 banks globally. Higher of G-SIB or O-SII applies.

definition: Sum of all CET1 buffers stacked above Pillar 1 minimums and P2R: Conservation + CCyB + SyRB + max(G-SIB, O-SII). All must be met with CET1 only. The CBR is what the MDA threshold tests against: dipping into the CBR triggers the distribution restrictions but is not itself a regulatory breach.
flashcardBack: Conservation + CCyB + SyRB + max(G-SIB, O-SII). CET1-only. Dipping into CBR triggers MDA but is not a regulatory breach.

definition: Tier 1 capital divided by total exposure (on- + off-balance-sheet, with derivative exposures grossed up). Non-risk-sensitive backstop to the risk-weighted ratios. Basel III minimum 3%; G-SIBs face surcharge (3.5–4.25%). Designed to prevent the 30–50× leverage that pre-crisis investment banks ran on low-risk-weight asset books – a Turner-Review reform.
flashcardBack: Tier 1 / total exposure. Non-risk-sensitive. Min 3%, G-SIBs higher. Backstop preventing pre-crisis 30–50× IB leverage.

definition: Automatic restriction triggered when a bank breaches its Combined Buffer Requirement. The MDA caps dividends, AT1 coupon payments, and discretionary bonuses, scaled by how deep the breach. Designed to make buffers usable in stress without bank management facing a fait-accompli capital crisis. The mechanism that operationalises the conservation-buffer concept.
flashcardBack: Cap on dividends, AT1 coupons, bonuses when CBR breached. Scaled by breach depth. Operationalises conservation buffer.

definition: FSB minimum loss-absorbing capacity for G-SIBs: 18% of RWA / 6.75% of leverage exposure from 2022. Comprises regulatory capital plus eligible bail-in-able liabilities, structurally subordinated to operating liabilities. The global counterpart to EU MREL but applied uniformly to G-SIBs rather than calibrated bank-by-bank.
flashcardBack: FSB G-SIB requirement: ≥18% RWA / 6.75% leverage exposure of bail-in-able capacity. Global counterpart to EU MREL.

definition: EU implementation of Basel III. The Regulation (CRR) is directly applicable; the Directive (CRD) requires national transposition. CRR covers Pillar 1 capital, leverage, large exposures; CRD covers supervisory powers, governance, buffers. CRR3 / CRD VI (in force from 2025) implements Basel III's final reforms including the output floor, revised credit-risk and operational-risk standards. Named in Finals 2024 Q3b grading guide.
flashcardBack: EU Basel III: CRR (regulation, P1+leverage+large exposures), CRD (directive, supervisory powers+buffers). CRR3/CRD VI from 2025 = output floor + revised standards.

definition: Basel III short-term liquidity rule: HQLA / net cash outflows over a 30-day stress scenario ≥ 100%. Stress assumptions include retail-deposit run-off, partial loss of wholesale funding, drawdowns on committed lines, and contractual derivative outflows. Designed to ensure the bank survives 30 days of severe stress without external support – long enough for resolution authorities to act.
flashcardBack: HQLA / 30-day stressed net outflow ≥ 100%. Survive 30 days unaided. Stress: retail run-off, wholesale loss, drawdowns, derivative outflows.

definition: Basel III structural-liquidity rule: Available Stable Funding (ASF) / Required Stable Funding (RSF) over a 1-year horizon ≥ 100%. ASF weights long-dated and retail funding more heavily; RSF weights illiquid long-duration assets more heavily. Forces banks to fund long assets with stable liabilities, addressing the maturity-mismatch fragility exposed by Northern Rock and SIVs.
flashcardBack: ASF / RSF (1y) ≥ 100%. Forces stable funding for long assets. Addresses Northern Rock / SIV maturity-mismatch fragility.

definition: Numerator of the LCR. Three levels with progressively heavier haircuts and concentration caps. Level 1: cash, central-bank reserves, top-rated sovereign bonds (no haircut, no cap). Level 2A: lower-rated sovereigns, top-rated corporate bonds (15% haircut, capped at 40% of HQLA). Level 2B: lower-rated corporates, equities, RMBS (25–50% haircut, capped at 15%).
flashcardBack: LCR numerator. L1: cash, reserves, top sovereigns (no haircut). L2A: 15% haircut, ≤40% cap. L2B: 25–50% haircut, ≤15% cap.

definition: NSFR mechanics. ASF = sum of liabilities × ASF factor (regulatory capital and >1y funding: 100%; stable retail deposits: 95%; less stable: 90%; <1y wholesale: 0–50%). RSF = sum of assets × RSF factor (cash 0%; <1y interbank 10%; performing residential mortgages 65%; performing corporate loans 85%; long-dated illiquid assets 100%). Ratio must be ≥ 100%.
flashcardBack: ASF: stable funding factors (capital/long debt 100%, retail 90–95%, wholesale 0–50%). RSF: asset-side factors (cash 0%, mortgages 65%, illiquid 100%). ASF/RSF ≥ 100%.

definition: Walter Bagehot's prescription for the LOLR in Lombard Street: in a panic, the central bank should lend freely, at a penalty rate, against good collateral. 'Freely' to break the panic; 'penalty rate' to deter abuse and ensure quick repayment; 'good collateral' to limit credit risk to the central bank. The doctrine remains the textbook standard for emergency liquidity 150 years on, although modern central banks have widened the collateral universe and softened penalty rates.
flashcardBack: Lend freely, at penalty rate, against good collateral. Bagehot 1873. Still the textbook LOLR standard, with modernised collateral and softer pricing.

definition: Norwegian liquidity facility deployed October 2008. Banks swapped illiquid covered bonds (OMF) for liquid Norwegian government Treasury bills, on a temporary basis. Provided NOK 230bn at peak – about 20% of GDP. Did not expand the central-bank balance sheet (a swap, not a loan). Considered the most successful single Norwegian crisis-response measure and a template for collateral-swap LOLR design.
flashcardBack: 2008 Norway: banks swapped OMF for govt T-bills. NOK 230bn / ~20% GDP. Balance-sheet-neutral (swap). Template for collateral-swap LOLR.

definition: Reciprocal currency arrangements between the Federal Reserve and select foreign central banks (ECB, BoE, BoJ, SNB, plus emerging-market partners). Activated October 2008 and again March 2020 to provide USD liquidity to non-US banks during dollar funding stress. Mechanism: foreign CB borrows USD from the Fed against its own currency, lends to its banks; reverses at maturity at the original spot rate (no FX risk to either CB).
flashcardBack: Fed↔foreign CB USD swap. Activated Oct 2008, Mar 2020. Foreign CB borrows USD vs domestic FX, lends on to banks. Cures dollar basis blowout.

definition: Self-fulfilling rise in repo haircuts during 2007–08 that functioned as a shadow-banking bank run. Counterparties demanded ever-larger collateral cushions on structured-credit collateral; banks unable to source incremental collateral were forced sellers, further depressing prices and raising haircuts. The mechanism was first articulated as a 'run' by Gorton & Metrick – repos are the wholesale equivalent of demand deposits.
flashcardBack: Repo haircuts spike 2007–08 → forced collateral sales → prices fall → haircuts rise. Wholesale-funding equivalent of bank run (Gorton & Metrick).

definition: Self-reinforcing loop linking funding liquidity and market liquidity. Falling collateral prices raise margins and haircuts (funding-liquidity stress) → leveraged investors are forced to sell (selling pressure) → prices fall further (market-liquidity stress) → margins rise again. The spiral runs in both directions but is particularly violent on the way down. Foundational shadow-banking-crisis mechanism.
flashcardBack: Falling prices → higher margins → forced sales → falling prices. Funding ↔ market liquidity loop. Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2009.

definition: Forced sale of assets at prices well below fundamental value, typically because the seller faces a binding liquidity or capital constraint. Externalises losses onto other holders of similar assets via mark-to-market accounting and contagion of haircuts. Central to GFC mechanics; tested in Spring 2024 Q3 grading guide verbatim. Mitigated by central-bank purchases or temporary accounting forbearance.
flashcardBack: Forced sale below fundamental value. Spreads losses via M2M accounting and haircut contagion. Spring 2024 Q3 verbatim. Mitigated by CB purchases / accounting forbearance.

term: Withdrawal-Risk Diversification / Law of Large Numbers
definition: Foundational reason demand-deposit funding is workable: with many uncorrelated small depositors, the law of large numbers makes aggregate withdrawals statistically predictable, and banks need to hold only a fraction in liquid form. The diversification breaks down when (a) deposits are concentrated (SVB: ~90% of deposits above the FDIC limit, in a tightly-networked tech-VC sector), or (b) withdrawals become correlated through panic (D-D bad equilibrium).
flashcardBack: LoLN: many small uncorrelated depositors → predictable outflows → fractional reserves work. Breaks under concentration (SVB) or correlated panic (D-D).

definition: Coordinated management of a bank's asset and liability sensitivities to interest rates, FX, credit, and liquidity. Outputs: gap reports (repricing maturity), duration analysis, EVE (Economic Value of Equity) and NII sensitivity, hedging programmes (swaps, FX forwards). Owned by a senior committee (ALCO). Cited verbatim in May 2025 Q2c grading guide.
flashcardBack: Coordinated rate/FX/credit/liquidity sensitivity management. Outputs: gap reports, EVE/NII sensitivities, hedge programmes. ALCO-owned. May 2025 Q2c verbatim.

definition: Bankruptcy-remote legal entity that holds pooled assets and issues tranched securities backed by those assets' cash flows. The originating bank legally sells the assets to the SPV, achieving (in true-sale structures) accounting derecognition and capital relief. The SPV has no employees and operates under a deed of trust managed by a trustee. Essential plumbing of all securitisations.
flashcardBack: Bankruptcy-remote pooling vehicle issuing tranched securities. True-sale to SPV achieves derecognition + capital relief. No employees, trustee-managed.

definition: Layered claims on an SPV's cash flows. Senior tranches are paid first and absorb losses last – typically AAA-rated. Mezzanine tranches (BBB) sit between. Equity tranches (first-loss, also called 'residual' or 'toxic waste') are paid last and absorb losses first; held to keep originator skin-in-the-game in some structures. Subordination is the primary credit-enhancement mechanism.
flashcardBack: Senior (AAA, last-loss), Mezzanine (BBB), Equity (first-loss, 'toxic waste'). Subordination = primary credit enhancement.

definition: Layering of claims so that junior tranches absorb losses before senior tranches. Primary credit-enhancement technique in securitisation. The thickness of subordinated layers below a senior tranche determines its rating: more subordination → more rating headroom for the senior. Pre-crisis modelling massively underestimated correlated subprime defaults, so 'safe' senior tranches received losses anyway.
flashcardBack: Junior tranches absorb losses first. Primary credit enhancement. Senior rating ≈ thickness of subordination beneath. Pre-crisis correlation models underestimated tail.

definition: Credit-enhancement mechanism in which the value of pooled collateral exceeds the notional value of issued tranches. The excess provides a cushion that absorbs losses before the most-junior tranche is hit. Typical OC levels in pre-crisis subprime structures were 5–15%; cushions evaporated within months as default rates spiked.
flashcardBack: Pool value > tranches issued. Cushion absorbed before junior tranche hit. Pre-crisis subprime: 5–15%, evaporated within months in 2007–08.

definition: Generic term for techniques that improve a securitisation tranche's credit profile. Internal: subordination, overcollateralisation, excess spread, reserve accounts. External: monoline insurance (MBIA, Ambac – most failed in the GFC), parent guarantees, surety bonds. Each adds rating capacity but transfers risk to a third party whose own creditworthiness becomes the new weak link.
flashcardBack: Internal: subordination, OC, excess spread, reserve account. External: monoline insurance, guarantees. External credit ≤ guarantor's own.

definition: Securitisation in which the originating bank retains the loans on its balance sheet but transfers credit risk to investors via CDS or financial guarantees referencing a reference pool. Achieves regulatory capital relief but NOT funding – a recurring T/F trap on the exam (Spring 2024 Q1e, May 2025 Q1b). Contrast with traditional 'true-sale' structures that achieve both. Used heavily today in 'significant risk transfer' (SRT) trades for capital optimisation.
flashcardBack: Loans stay on bank B/S; risk transferred via CDS on reference pool. Capital relief YES, funding NO. T/F trap on every recent paper. SRT trades today.

definition: Loans are legally sold to a bankruptcy-remote SPV, which funds the purchase by issuing tranched securities. Achieves both funding (cash for the originator) and capital relief (assets derecognised). Pre-crisis dominant model for MBS, ABS, and CDOs. Post-crisis structures retain risk via originator's holding of equity tranche (skin-in-the-game requirement under Article 6 CRR).
flashcardBack: Legal sale to SPV → both funding AND capital relief. Pre-crisis dominant. Post-crisis: originator retains equity tranche (skin in the game).

definition: Lending model in which the originator does not retain the credit risk of loans it makes – it sells them on into securitisation pipelines. Reduces the originator's incentive to screen borrowers carefully and to monitor afterwards (moral hazard). Identified as a structural cause of subprime-mortgage quality collapse. Post-crisis 'skin-in-the-game' rules (5% retention requirement) are a direct OTD reform.
flashcardBack: Originator sells the loan and the credit risk. Weakens screening and monitoring incentives. Subprime-quality collapse cause. Cured by 5% skin-in-the-game.

definition: A CDO whose collateral pool consists of mezzanine tranches of other CDOs (typically BBB MBS tranches). Re-tranches the BBB pool, manufacturing new senior AAA-rated tranches from collateral that itself was already low-quality. Created enormous nominal AAA volumes from a thin layer of subprime mortgages and concealed correlation risk: a small shock to subprime defaults propagated nonlinearly through the structure. Emblematic of pre-crisis structuring excess.
flashcardBack: CDO of CDO mezzanine tranches. Re-tranches BBB → manufactures AAA from subprime. Hidden correlation risk; nonlinear propagation of subprime default shocks.

definition: Short-term debt (typically 1–270 days) issued by SIVs and conduits, backed by a pool of receivables and other ABS. Funded the maturity-mismatched shadow-banking system. The ABCP market froze on 9 August 2007 after BNP Paribas suspended redemptions on three subprime-exposed funds; SIVs lost the ability to roll, forcing sponsor banks to absorb assets back onto their balance sheets. Widely regarded as the start of the GFC.
flashcardBack: Short-term (1–270d) commercial paper backed by ABS pool. Funded SIVs/conduits. Market froze 9 Aug 2007 (BNP Paribas trigger) – start of GFC.

definition: SIV-like off-balance-sheet vehicle sponsored by a bank, funding ABS purchases with ABCP. Distinguishing feature from a SIV: usually has full liquidity backstop from the sponsor bank. When ABCP markets froze in 2007, the backstops triggered, returning the assets and funding need to the sponsor's balance sheet – a pre-arranged transmission of shadow-banking stress to the regulated sector.
flashcardBack: Off-B/S ABCP-funded vehicle, with sponsor liquidity backstop (unlike SIVs). Backstops triggered Aug 2007 → assets reabsorbed onto sponsor balance sheet.

definition: Pre-crisis acronym for 'No Income, No Job, No Assets' subprime mortgages. Extreme example of the documentation and underwriting collapse in US 2003–07 mortgage origination. Made possible by originate-to-distribute incentives, broker-driven origination paid on volume, and AAA-rated securitisation that absorbed any quality. Iconic crisis-cause illustration.
flashcardBack: 'No Income, No Job, No Assets' subprime mortgages, 2003–07. Documentation/underwriting collapse enabled by OTD + broker volume pay + AAA securitisation.

definition: US residential mortgages extended to borrowers with weak credit histories, low income documentation, or high loan-to-value ratios. Subprime origination peaked around $600bn in 2006. Securitisation into private-label MBS – and re-securitisation into CDO and CDO² – was the proximate trigger of the GFC. The asset class's losses were not the largest in absolute terms, but its complexity and opacity made it the catalyst of broader panic.
flashcardBack: Weak-credit US mortgages. Peaked ~$600bn in 2006. Securitised via private-label MBS / CDO / CDO² – proximate GFC trigger via complexity and opacity.

definition: Three big credit-rating agencies (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) rate structured products on an issuer-pays basis: the issuer chooses and pays the agency. Identified as a structural conflict of interest in the pre-crisis system: agencies competed on rating leniency for repeat business, particularly in lucrative structured-credit volumes. Dodd-Frank and the EU Credit Rating Agency Regulation responded with tighter governance, methodology disclosure, and limited liability changes, but the issuer-pays model survives.
flashcardBack: Big 3 (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) – issuer-pays. Structural conflict: rating leniency for repeat business, particularly in structured credit. Dodd-Frank/EU CRA Regulation tightened but model survives.

triage_reason: Reserve Primary Fund "broke the buck" – lecture footnote
term: Money Market Mutual Fund (MMF) / Reserve Primary Fund 'Breaking the Buck'
definition: MMFs are open-end funds investing in short-term high-quality money-market instruments, marketed to retail and corporate cash investors as cash-equivalent at $1 NAV. The Reserve Primary Fund – a $62bn MMF – broke the buck on 16 September 2008 (NAV dropped to $0.97) after Lehman's failure devalued its CP holdings. Triggered an industry-wide MMF run, contained only by an unprecedented Treasury blanket guarantee on MMF deposits.
flashcardBack: Reserve Primary Fund NAV→$0.97 on 16 Sept 2008 from Lehman CP. First MMF buck-break since 1994. Industry run cured by Treasury blanket guarantee.

definition: No-arbitrage relation between spot and forward FX rates: F = S × (1 + r_quote × t/360) / (1 + r_base × t/360). If CIP holds, borrowing in one currency and swapping into another yields no risk-free profit. Held tightly pre-2008, broke down persistently afterwards (the cross-currency basis), reflecting balance-sheet costs of arbitrage and dollar-funding scarcity. Tested numerically on Spring 2024 Q4a.
flashcardBack: F = S × (1 + r_q t/360)/(1 + r_b t/360). Tight pre-2008, persistent post-2008 deviation = cross-currency basis = balance-sheet cost / USD scarcity. Spring 2024 Q4a.

definition: Spot rate (S): exchange rate for delivery in T+2. Forward rate (F): rate agreed today for delivery on a future date (T+1m, 3m, 6m, 1y, etc.). The forward is not a forecast of the future spot – it is the no-arbitrage rate implied by interest-rate differentials via CIP. Forward 'premium' (F > S) means the quote currency has lower interest rates than the base.
flashcardBack: S = T+2 delivery. F = future-date delivery, set by CIP not forecast. Forward premium F>S ⇔ quote has lower r than base.

definition: Forward minus spot: F − S, quoted in pips. Compensates for the interest-rate differential implied by CIP. A positive swap point (forward premium) means the foreign currency trades at a higher forward price than spot – typically because the foreign currency offers lower interest rates. Swap points are the standard quoting convention in interbank FX-forward markets. Direct numerical answer expected on May 2024 Q4a.
flashcardBack: F − S, in pips. CIP-implied compensation for rate differential. Positive points = foreign currency forward premium = foreign rates lower. May 2024 Q4a numeric.

definition: Long-dated derivative in which two parties exchange floating-rate payments in different currencies, with notional principal exchanged at the same spot rate at inception and at maturity (no FX exposure on principal). Typical structure: pay USD floating (SOFR), receive EUR floating (€STR), with the CCBS basis spread added to one leg as compensation for deviation from CIP. Primary tool for hedging structural FX-funding mismatches (e.g. EUR-funded NOK lending).
flashcardBack: Long-dated swap of floating legs in two currencies; principal exchanged at same spot in/out (no FX risk). Basis spread added for CIP deviation. Hedges structural FX funding.

definition: Spread added to one leg of a CCBS to enforce no-arbitrage when CIP is violated. A negative dollar basis means receiving USD floating costs less than CIP implies – equivalently, those funding via FX swap pay a premium to access dollars. Blew out to several hundred basis points in 2008 and again March 2020. Cured by Fed swap lines, which arbitrage the basis directly via central-bank-to-central-bank dollar provision.
flashcardBack: CCBS leg adjustment for CIP deviation. Negative dollar basis = USD funding premium via FX swap. Blew out 2008, Mar 2020. Cured by Fed swap lines.

definition: Same-currency swap of one interest-rate exposure for another, typically fixed-for-floating. Notional principal is not exchanged (only interest payments). Transforms but does not eliminate interest-rate risk: a fixed-rate payer locks in funding cost but takes the risk that floating rates fall below contracted fixed. Building block of bank ALM, fixed-rate mortgage funding, and combined EUR-IRS + CCBS hedges of foreign-bond issuance into NOK-floating.
flashcardBack: Same-currency fixed-floating swap. Notional not exchanged. Transforms, not eliminates, IR risk. ALM building block; fixed mortgage funding; NOK-bond issuance hedge.

definition: Reference rates underlying floating-rate instruments. LIBOR (London, USD/GBP/JPY/CHF/EUR): unsecured interbank survey rate, discontinued 2021–23 after manipulation scandals and shrinking interbank volumes. Successor risk-free rates: SOFR (USD, secured, repo-based), SONIA (GBP, unsecured overnight), TONA (JPY), SARON (CHF), €STR (EUR, unsecured overnight). EURIBOR (term, hybrid methodology) survives. NIBOR (Norwegian Interbank Offered Rate) is the NOK benchmark – survey-based, similar to LIBOR but ongoing.
flashcardBack: LIBOR (gone) → SOFR (USD), €STR (EUR), SONIA (GBP), TONA (JPY), SARON (CHF). EURIBOR survives. NIBOR is NOK benchmark.

triage_reason: lecture 9 – not in past finals as standalone
definition: Clearing house that interposes itself between the two parties to a derivative trade, becoming buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer. Mutualises and centralises counterparty credit risk, enforces variation and initial margin, and operates a default waterfall (defaulter's margin → guaranty fund → CCP capital → mutualised survivor contributions). Mandatory clearing of standardised OTC derivatives is a Dodd-Frank / EMIR post-crisis reform. Cited verbatim in May 2025 Q1a grading guide ('Central Counterparty Clearing House').
flashcardBack: Clearing house: buyer to every seller, seller to every buyer. Variation + initial margin, default waterfall. Mandatory for standard OTC since Dodd-Frank/EMIR. May 2025 Q1a.

definition: Collateral posted on derivative positions to mitigate counterparty risk. Initial margin (IM): up-front posted against potential future exposure (typically 99% 10-day VaR). Variation margin (VM): posted daily as MTM moves (one-for-one settlement of yesterday's gain/loss). A margin call demands additional VM when the position has moved against the holder. Mandatory uncleared-margin rules (UMR) extended IM to non-cleared OTC trades from 2017–22.
flashcardBack: IM: up-front PFE buffer. VM: daily MTM settlement. Margin call = top-up demand after adverse move. UMR extended IM to non-cleared OTC 2017–22.

definition: Mechanism by which currency depreciation triggers further depreciation through hedge rebalancing. A foreign investor holds a NOK bond hedged with an EUR/NOK forward sized to the bond's NOK value. When NOK falls, the bond's NOK value (in EUR terms) is now larger than the hedge – under-hedged. Rebalancing requires selling more NOK forward, which pushes NOK lower further. Documented driver of the March 2020 NOK collapse.
flashcardBack: NOK falls → foreign-investor hedge becomes too small → sells more NOK forward → NOK falls further. Self-reinforcing FX-depreciation loop. Mar 2020 NOK.

definition: Companion mechanism to the rebalancing channel. NOK depreciation produced adverse mark-to-market on FX hedges (sold-NOK-forward positions lost value as NOK fell). To meet variation-margin calls in the foreign currency, hedgers sold Norwegian krone-denominated bonds for cash, which pushed NOK bond yields up and NOK lower. Identified by Norges Bank and Alstadheim's guest lecture as a primary driver of the March 2020 turbulence.
flashcardBack: NOK fall → FX-hedge MTM loss → margin calls met by selling NOK bonds → bond prices fall, NOK falls further. Mar 2020 driver per Norges Bank.

definition: Persistent post-2008 phenomenon in which non-US banks face structural difficulty borrowing dollars in unsecured markets, manifesting as a negative cross-currency basis. Driven by US money-fund regulatory reform (2014 reform pushed prime funds to government), Volcker Rule constraints on US-bank inventory, and balance-sheet costs of FX-swap arbitrage. Acute episodes 2008 and March 2020 cured only by Fed swap lines.
flashcardBack: Structural post-2008 USD funding scarcity → negative cross-currency basis. Drivers: MMF reform, Volcker, B/S costs. Acute Aug 2008, Mar 2020 → Fed swap lines.

definition: Bilateral, OTC agreement to exchange an asset on a future date at a price agreed today. Foundational derivative on which FX swaps, IRS, and CCBS are built. No initial cash flow (in standard form); MTM accumulates over the life of the contract; settlement at maturity. Counterparty risk is symmetric – either party can be in the money. Distinguished from futures by being OTC, customised, and uncleared (margin requirements vary).
flashcardBack: OTC bilateral future-date exchange at today's agreed price. No initial cash flow; MTM accumulates; settles at maturity. OTC vs cleared/standardised futures.

definition: EU directive (2014/59/EU, BRRD2 from 2019) establishing the bank-resolution framework. Components: failing-or-likely-to-fail trigger; public-interest assessment; four resolution tools (sale of business, bridge institution, asset separation, bail-in); MREL requirement; resolution-planning duties. Replaced ad-hoc bailout-with-state-aid responses. Tested on every recent GRA6546 final.
flashcardBack: EU 2014 directive: FOLF trigger, public-interest assessment, four tools, MREL, resolution planning. Replaced bailouts. On every recent final.

definition: Bank-drafted, supervisor-approved plan of self-help measures the bank would take to restore viability before reaching the resolution threshold. Standard menu: capital raising, dividend suspension, AT1 coupon cancellation, divestments, deleveraging, liability-management exercises. Updated annually. Tested directly on Final 2024 Q6 vs the resolution plan.
flashcardBack: Bank-drafted self-help plan: raise capital, suspend dividends, divest, deleverage. Supervisor-approved, annual. Final 2024 Q6 vs resolution plan.

definition: Resolution-authority-drafted plan setting out how a failing bank would be resolved if FOLF and the public-interest test were met.
