Identifies preferred resolution strategy (bail-in / sale / bridge / separation), critical functions to preserve, MREL calibration, and operational dependencies. Maintained by the SRB for significant banks, by Finanstilsynet for Norwegian institutions. Tested directly on Final 2024 Q6.
flashcardBack: Authority-drafted plan executed if FOLF + public interest. Sets preferred tool, critical functions, MREL, operational deps. SRB / Finanstilsynet. Final 2024 Q6.

definition: BRRD trigger condition for resolution. Four limbs (any one suffices): (1) authorisation to operate has been or is likely to be withdrawn; (2) liabilities exceed or are likely to exceed assets; (3) the bank cannot or is likely to be unable to pay debts as they fall due (cash-flow insolvency); (4) the bank requires or is likely to require extraordinary public financial support. Memorise verbatim – May 2025 Q6b.
flashcardBack: Four limbs: lost authorisation / liabilities>assets / cash-flow insolvency / requires extraordinary public support. Any one triggers resolution. May 2025 Q6b.

definition: Test that determines whether a FOLF bank goes into resolution (using the BRRD toolkit) or into normal liquidation. Resolution is in the public interest only if liquidation would not preserve critical functions, financial stability, depositor protection, or public funds. If the public-interest test fails, the bank is liquidated under national insolvency law and the deposit guarantee scheme pays out covered depositors.
flashcardBack: Resolution vs liquidation test. Resolution only if liquidation can't preserve critical functions/stability/depositors/funds. Else liquidation + DGS payout.

definition: Four statutory tools the resolution authority can deploy on a FOLF bank in the public interest: (1) Sale of Business – transfer to a private buyer; (2) Bridge Institution – temporary public entity holding the bank's operations; (3) Asset Separation – bad-bank carve-out (only in conjunction with another tool); (4) Bail-in – write down/convert liabilities to recapitalise. Tools can be combined. Examiner expects all four named.
flashcardBack: (1) Sale of Business, (2) Bridge Institution, (3) Asset Separation, (4) Bail-in. Combinable. Examiner expects all four named.

definition: BRRD resolution tool: transfer of all or part of the failing bank's business – shares, assets, rights, liabilities – to a willing private acquirer, without shareholder consent. Used by the SRB on Sberbank Europe in March 2022, completed within days of FOLF determination. Standard preferred tool when a viable acquirer exists, because it preserves the franchise and avoids public-balance-sheet exposure.
flashcardBack: Transfer to private buyer without shareholder consent. SRB used on Sberbank Europe Mar 2022 within days. Preferred when viable acquirer exists.

definition: BRRD resolution tool: temporary public entity created to hold all or part of the failing bank's operations until a permanent solution (sale, run-down, restructuring) is arranged. Bridge has a maximum two-year initial life, extendable by one year at a time. Allows continuity of critical functions while the resolution authority works on a permanent disposition. Standard tool when no immediate buyer is available.
flashcardBack: Temporary public entity, max 2y (extendable). Holds operations while authority arranges permanent disposition. Used when no immediate buyer.

definition: BRRD resolution tool: transfer of assets (typically toxic, illiquid, or non-core) to a publicly-controlled Asset Management Vehicle (AMV) so the 'good bank' continues with a clean book. Cannot be used as the only tool – must be combined with sale of business, bridge institution, or bail-in. Iconic precursor: Sweden's Securum and Retriva in the 1992 Nordic crisis.
flashcardBack: Bad-bank carve-out into AMV. Cannot be used alone – must combine with another tool. Securum/Retriva (Sweden 1992) is the model.

definition: First component of MREL: the capital needed to absorb losses on the way down to resolution, calibrated approximately as the bank's current capital requirement (Pillar 1 + P2R + Combined Buffer Requirement). Captures the loss-absorption need before any recapitalisation begins.
flashcardBack: MREL component for losses on the way down ≈ P1 + P2R + CBR. Pre-recapitalisation loss absorption.

definition: Second component of MREL: the capital needed to restore the bank – or a successor entity – to its full operating capital requirement post-resolution, so it can continue as a going concern. Calibrated similarly to LAA but applied on the post-resolution balance sheet (which may be smaller after asset transfers).
flashcardBack: MREL component to rebuild capital to full operating level post-resolution. Applied to post-resolution (possibly shrunken) balance sheet.

definition: Going-concern: capital absorbs losses while the bank continues to operate as a viable entity. CET1 absorbs first; AT1 absorbs at trigger (typically 5.125%/7% CET1) via write-down or conversion. Gone-concern: capital absorbs only at the point of non-viability or in resolution. Tier 2, senior non-preferred, and senior unsecured fall here. The distinction is the conceptual backbone of the bail-in waterfall and AT1 instrument design.
flashcardBack: Going-concern: bank still operating (CET1 always; AT1 at trigger). Gone-concern: at PONV/resolution (T2, SNP, senior). Backbone of bail-in design.

definition: Bond class created explicitly to be bail-in-able under BRRD. Ranks below ordinary senior unsecured but above subordinated debt in the creditor hierarchy. The 'senior non-preferred' label flags to investors that, despite being senior, the instrument is designed to absorb losses before non-preferred deposits and ordinary senior unsecured. France introduced the class in 2016; Norway has its own SNP framework. Explicit line on the Lilledal Sparebank balance sheet on May 2025 Q6.
flashcardBack: Senior bond class designed to be bail-in-able. Below senior unsecured, above subordinated. Lilledal Sparebank on May 2025 Q6.

definition: Statutory ranking of claims in resolution and liquidation, from most-protected to first-loss: covered deposits (super-preference) → uninsured retail and SME deposits (preference) → ordinary senior unsecured → senior non-preferred → Tier 2 → AT1 → CET1 (equity). Bail-in writes down from the bottom up. Spring 2024 Q5 asks for the ranking explicitly; understanding this hierarchy is essential to every recovery/resolution question.
flashcardBack: Top→bottom: covered deposits → preferred deposits → senior unsecured → SNP → T2 → AT1 → equity. Bail-in writes down bottom-up. Spring 2024 Q5 verbatim.

definition: Top-of-hierarchy ranking for deposit-guarantee-covered deposits (NOK 2m in Norway, €100k in EU) in resolution and liquidation. Introduced in Norwegian law from 2019 implementing BRRD2. Means the deposit guarantee scheme – having paid out covered depositors – recovers from the estate ahead of all other creditors. Final 2023 Q2 was a 20-point essay on the consequences of removing super-preference: higher cost of senior unsecured funding, weakened bail-in chain, larger DGS exposure.
flashcardBack: Covered deposits at very top of hierarchy. Norway 2019 (BRRD2). DGS recovers ahead of all creditors. Final 2023 Q2 was 20-pt essay.

definition: Centralised EU resolution authority for significant banks in the Banking Union (eurozone-21 + opted-in member states). Established 2014, fully operational from 2016. Maintains resolution plans, calibrates MREL, and executes resolution decisions for ~120 banks. Resolved Banco Popular (June 2017, sold to Santander for €1) and Sberbank Europe (March 2022, Sale of Business within days).
flashcardBack: Centralised EU resolution authority for significant banks (~120 in Banking Union). Resolved Banco Popular (Jun 2017 → Santander €1) and Sberbank Europe (Mar 2022).

term: Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM) / Single Resolution Fund (SRF)
definition: SRM is the institutional framework for centralised bank resolution in the Banking Union: SRB at the core plus national resolution authorities. The SRF is its mutualised funding pool, financed by ex-ante contributions from Banking-Union banks; target size is 1% of covered deposits (~€80bn at full build-out, reached December 2023). Used to support the resolution toolkit (e.g., backstop the bridge institution).
flashcardBack: SRM = SRB + national authorities (Banking Union). SRF = mutualised fund, ex-ante bank levies, target 1% covered deposits (~€80bn, full from Dec 2023).

term: Too Big to Fail (TBTF) / Implicit Government Guarantee
definition: Pre-crisis market belief that systemic banks would be bailed out rather than allowed to fail, so that their senior debt was implicitly backed by the sovereign. Quantified as a funding-cost subsidy (e.g., IMF estimated 60–80bp for the largest US banks pre-2008). Bail-in / MREL / TLAC were designed explicitly to break this expectation. Tested on every recent finals paper as 'Why is bail-in a remedy to TBTF?'
flashcardBack: Pre-crisis belief big banks always rescued → funding subsidy 60–80bp. Bail-in / MREL / TLAC are direct remedies. On every recent finals paper.

definition: Recapitalisation of a failing bank using external (taxpayer) funds – government equity injections, asset purchases, blanket guarantees. The pre-crisis norm and the policy used through 2008–10 (TARP, RBS/Lloyds nationalisations, Norwegian Statens finansfond). Bail-in is the post-crisis replacement. Direct T/F on May 2025 Q1c. Common pairing question: 'Distinguish bail-in and bail-out.'
flashcardBack: Recap with taxpayer funds – TARP, RBS/Lloyds, Statens finansfond. Pre-crisis norm. Replaced by bail-in. May 2025 Q1c T/F.

term: Single Point of Entry (SPE) vs Multiple Point of Entry (MPE)
definition: Two strategic resolution approaches for cross-border banking groups. SPE: resolution applied at the parent (top-of-the-house); losses pushed up from subsidiaries via internal MREL; one resolution authority leads. MPE: resolution applied at multiple subsidiary entities in their host jurisdictions; pre-positioned local capital; multiple authorities. SPE typical for centralised groups (HSBC, Santander); MPE for federated groups (Nordea historically). Choice is a key element of the resolution plan.
flashcardBack: SPE: parent-level resolution, losses pushed up via internal MREL, one authority. MPE: subsidiary-level resolution, pre-positioned local capital, multiple authorities.

definition: Trigger for statutory write-down or conversion of AT1 and Tier 2 instruments outside resolution proper. PONV is reached when the resolution authority determines the bank would no longer be viable absent the action – typically just before formal FOLF and resolution. The PONV write-down/conversion is the legal hook by which AT1 and T2 contribute loss absorption ahead of bail-in proper.
flashcardBack: Trigger for AT1/T2 statutory write-down/conversion just before formal resolution. Hook for AT1 and T2 loss absorption.

term: No Creditor Worse Off than in Liquidation (NCWO / NCWOL)
definition: BRRD safeguard principle: no creditor or shareholder should incur greater losses in resolution than they would have suffered if the bank had been liquidated under normal insolvency law. If they do, they have a right to compensation from the resolution fund. The NCWO test was central to the legal challenges to the Credit Suisse AT1 write-down – bondholders argued the write-down was inconsistent with NCWO given equity holders received UBS shares.
flashcardBack: BRRD safeguard: no creditor worse off than in liquidation. If breached → compensation from SRF. Centre of Credit Suisse AT1 legal challenges.

triage_reason: SVB systemic-risk exception – used in case studies
definition: US FDIC tool allowing the agency to exceed the 'least-cost resolution' standard when needed to prevent serious systemic consequences. Invoked on 12 March 2023 following SVB's failure to guarantee all uninsured deposits at SVB and Signature Bank – protecting balances above the $250k FDIC limit. Controversial because it created a de facto unlimited deposit insurance for similar runs.
flashcardBack: US FDIC tool to exceed least-cost standard for systemic reasons. Used 12 Mar 2023 to guarantee all SVB/Signature uninsured deposits – de facto unlimited DI.

definition: Federal Reserve emergency facility launched 12 March 2023 in response to SVB's failure. Lent to banks for up to one year against high-quality collateral valued at par (rather than market) – directly addressing the HTM-loss / fire-sale problem that took down SVB. Terminated for new advances on 11 March 2024. Innovation: par-value collateral haircuts violate Bagehot's 'good collateral' principle but were necessary to break the run dynamic.
flashcardBack: Fed emergency facility, Mar 2023–Mar 2024. Lend 1y vs par-valued collateral – addresses HTM-loss problem. Violates Bagehot's good-collateral rule by design.

definition: Norwegian Financial Supervisory Authority. Single supervisor for banks, insurers, securities firms, and pension funds in Norway. Acts as both prudential supervisor and the Norwegian resolution authority under BRRD-implementing legislation. Operates the SREP, sets P2R, approves recovery plans, drafts resolution plans, and executes resolution. Intervened pre-emptively in the Næringsbanken case (2022–23).
flashcardBack: Norwegian FSA + resolution authority. Single supervisor for banks/insurers/securities. SREP, P2R, recovery+resolution plans. Intervened in Næringsbanken 2022–23.

triage_reason: 2024 Q3b post-2008 reforms – listed but not deep-tested
definition: UK structural reform implementing the Independent Commission on Banking (Vickers Report 2011). Required UK banking groups with retail deposits above £25bn to legally separate ring-fenced retail banking from investment banking and wholesale activities. Aim: protect deposit-taking from trading losses and simplify resolution. In force from January 2019. Listed in Finals 2024 Q3b grading guide.
flashcardBack: UK Vickers reform. Ring-fenced retail banking legally separated from IB/wholesale (>£25bn deposits). In force Jan 2019. Finals 2024 Q3b.

triage_reason: 2024 Q3b post-2008 reforms – listed but not deep-tested
definition: Section 619 of the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act: prohibits US insured-deposit banks from proprietary trading and from sponsoring or investing in hedge funds and private-equity funds (with exemptions for market-making, hedging, government-securities trading). Aim: separate trading risk from deposit-funded banking. Diluted progressively post-2018. Listed in Finals 2024 Q3b grading guide.
flashcardBack: Dodd-Frank §619. Bans US insured banks from prop trading + hedge/PE sponsorship. Diluted post-2018. Finals 2024 Q3b.

definition: Pre-emptive Finanstilsynet intervention in a small Norwegian bank: imposed a loan-origination freeze, raised P2R, and forced a recapitalisation, all before the FOLF threshold was reached. Considered an example of effective early supervisory action that avoided full resolution. Cited in topics.json bank-resolution and bank-crises content.
flashcardBack: Pre-emptive Finanstilsynet intervention 2022–23: lending freeze + P2R increase + forced recap. Avoided FOLF/resolution. Effective early supervision.

definition: European subsidiary of Russian Sberbank, hit by a sanctions-driven deposit run after Russia invaded Ukraine. Determined FOLF on 27 February 2022; SRB applied the Sale of Business tool within days, transferring Croatian and Slovenian operations to local buyers and unwinding the Austrian parent. Standard example of fast, decisive resolution under BRRD using the SoB tool.
flashcardBack: Sanctions-driven run on Russian Sberbank's EU sub, Feb 2022. SRB used Sale of Business within days. Standard fast-resolution case.

definition: Swiss authorities orchestrated UBS's takeover of Credit Suisse on 19 March 2023 after a deposit run accelerated post-SVB. Package: CHF 100bn liquidity assistance from SNB, CHF 9bn government loss guarantee, suspension of normal corporate governance to bypass shareholder votes. Crucially, FINMA wrote down CHF 16bn of CS AT1 to zero while UBS shareholders received shares – inverting the bail-in waterfall and triggering the NCWO controversy. Used Swiss resolution law, not BRRD.
flashcardBack: 19 Mar 2023: UBS takeover w/ CHF 100bn liquidity + CHF 9bn loss guarantee. AT1 zeroed before equity → NCWO controversy. Swiss law, not BRRD.

triage_reason: 2023 Q2 / 2025 mid Q3 – Norway DI fund
definition: Norwegian deposit guarantee and resolution-financing scheme. Coverage: NOK 2m per depositor per bank – significantly more generous than the EU €100k. Two pots: a deposit-guarantee fund and a resolution fund. Funded ex-ante through risk-adjusted levies on member banks (proposal: riskiest pays 20× safest from 2026, currently 12×). Direct 20-point essay on Feb 2025 Q3 and Final 2023 Q2.
flashcardBack: NOK 2m per depositor per bank (vs EU €100k). Two funds (DGS + resolution). Risk-adjusted ex-ante levies. Feb 2025 Q3 + Final 2023 Q2 = 20-pt essays.

triage_reason: EU DI framework – testable in 2023 Q2-style essay
definition: EU directive (2014/49/EU) harmonising national deposit-insurance schemes. Coverage ceiling: €100,000 per depositor per institution. Ex-ante funded by member-bank levies; target fund size 0.8% of covered deposits. Payout deadline: 7 working days from FOLF determination (down from 20 pre-2014). Information disclosure to depositors mandatory. Coverage comparison Norway-vs-EU is on every paper.
flashcardBack: EU 2014. €100k cap, 7-day payout, ex-ante 0.8% of covered deposits target. Norway-vs-EU comparison on every paper.

definition: Levies on member banks calibrated to bank-specific risk profile (capital, asset quality, funding stability) rather than flat-rate. Partial mitigant of the moral-hazard problem identified by Merton (1977): flat-rate premiums let risky banks free-ride on safe ones. In Norway, the riskiest bank currently pays 12× the safest; a 2026 proposal increases this to 20×. Standard example of structural fix to deposit-insurance moral hazard.
flashcardBack: Levies scaled to bank-specific risk. Mitigates Merton 1977 moral hazard. Norway: riskiest pays 12× safest, → 20× from 2026.

definition: Secured bonds issued by a bank or specialist issuer, backed by a dynamic cover pool of mortgages or public-sector loans. Bondholders have dual recourse: to the issuer and, on issuer default, to the cover pool ahead of unsecured creditors. AAA-rated under Standardised approach with low risk weight (10% in EU). Central to Norwegian bank funding and to the 2008–09 Bytteordning swap. Norwegian acronym: OMF (Obligasjoner med Fortrinnsrett – bonds with priority).
flashcardBack: Secured bonds, dual recourse to issuer + cover pool. AAA, 10% RW. Core Norwegian funding instrument; central to 2008 Bytteordning. NOR: OMF.

term: Merton (1977) – Deposit Insurance as Put Option
definition: Robert Merton showed that deposit insurance can be priced as a put option written by the insurer (state) on the bank's assets, with strike equal to insured-deposit liabilities. Implication: the insurance premium should rise with asset volatility σ and with leverage D/A. A flat-rate premium therefore underprices risky and highly-levered banks, transferring value from safe banks (and ultimately taxpayers) to risky ones. Theoretical foundation for risk-based premiums and the Marcus 1984 charter-value extension.
flashcardBack: DI = put option on bank assets, strike = insured deposits. Premium ↑ in σ and D/A. Flat-rate premiums underprice risky banks. Foundation for risk-based premiums.

definition: Transversal risk-and-disclosure framework integrating environmental (climate, biodiversity), social (labour, communities), and governance (board, ethics) factors into bank risk management. Channels: credit risk (loan-book exposure to transition/physical), market risk, operational risk, reputational. EBA Guidelines on ESG Risk Management (2025) formalise integration into ICAAP/SREP. Direct 15-point question on May 2025 Q5; high probability for May 2026.
flashcardBack: Transversal risk: environmental, social, governance – channelled via credit/market/operational/reputational risk. EBA Guidelines 2025. 15-pt May 2025 Q5.

definition: ESG-environmental risk channel from physical climate impacts. Acute: extreme weather events – floods, storms, wildfires, heatwaves – that destroy or impair collateral and disrupt borrowers (e.g. 2023 Norwegian flooding). Chronic: long-term shifts – sea-level rise, temperature trends, precipitation changes – that erode the economics of locations and assets (e.g. ski resorts, Mediterranean agriculture). Both feed into PD, LGD, and EAD over different horizons. Direct on May 2025 Q5b grading guide.
flashcardBack: Acute: extreme weather (storms, floods, fires). Chronic: long-term shifts (sea level, temperature, precipitation). Both feed PD/LGD/EAD. May 2025 Q5b.

definition: ESG-environmental risk from the shift to a low-carbon economy. Regulatory: carbon pricing, fossil-fuel bans, building-efficiency mandates erode borrower margins. Market: shifting demand and technology (EV uptake destroys ICE-vehicle residual values). Reputational: lender called out for financing controversial sectors (oil sands, coal). Manifests as stranded assets on bank loan books. Direct on May 2025 Q5b.
flashcardBack: Regulatory (carbon pricing, bans), Market (demand/tech shift), Reputational (financed-sector backlash). Manifests as stranded assets. May 2025 Q5b.

definition: Assets – typically fossil-fuel reserves, fossil-power plants, ICE-vehicle production, energy-inefficient buildings – that become economically uneconomic ahead of their physical useful life under the low-carbon transition. Carry-forward write-downs hit owner balance sheets; for banks, the credit-risk impact arrives through borrower distress before the asset is formally written off. Featured in May 2025 Q5b answer template and topics.json esg.
flashcardBack: Fossil/inefficient assets uneconomic before useful life ends. Bank channel: borrower distress → impairment. May 2025 Q5b answer template.

definition: Climate-disclosure frameworks. TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, 2017): voluntary framework for governance/strategy/risk-management/metrics&targets disclosure, now widely adopted. CSRD (EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, in force 2024): mandatory ESG reporting under European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). Double materiality (CSRD principle): firms report both how sustainability issues affect them (financial materiality) and how they affect society/environment (impact materiality).
flashcardBack: TCFD (2017, voluntary, 4 pillars). CSRD (EU 2024, mandatory, ESRS). Double materiality = financial AND impact-on-society reporting (CSRD principle).

term: EBA Guidelines on ESG Risk Management
definition: European Banking Authority guidelines (final 2025) requiring banks to integrate ESG risks into governance, business-model strategy, risk appetite, ICAAP, ILAAP, credit risk-management, and disclosure. Applies to all CRR-regulated banks, with proportionality. Operationalises ESG within the SREP. Together with CSRD they form the EU's bank-supervisory ESG architecture. Source-of-rules anchor in any ESG exam answer.
flashcardBack: EBA 2025: integrate ESG into governance/strategy/risk appetite/ICAAP/ILAAP/credit/disclosure. Applies to all CRR banks. Operationalises ESG in SREP.

term: Bernanke (1983) – Non-Monetary Effects of Bank Failures
definition: Ben Bernanke argued that bank failures during the Great Depression had real-economy effects beyond the contraction of money supply emphasised by Friedman & Schwartz. Failures destroyed bank-specific intermediation capital – relationships, credit assessments, monitoring infrastructure – that could not be quickly rebuilt by markets or by surviving banks. The credit-supply collapse extended and deepened the depression. Foundation of the modern case for aggressive crisis intervention. Motivated the 2022 Nobel Prize.
flashcardBack: Bank failures destroy intermediation capital → real-economy credit collapse beyond money-supply effects. Justifies aggressive crisis intervention. 2022 Nobel.

definition: UK mortgage lender heavily reliant on wholesale and securitisation funding (deposits funded only ~25% of assets). The August 2007 ABCP freeze cut Northern Rock off from rolling its funding; news of an LOLR approach to the Bank of England triggered queues outside branches on 14 September – the first UK bank run since 1866. Nationalised in February 2008. Standard case study for funding-mix fragility and the limits of LOLR communications.
flashcardBack: UK 2007: wholesale-dependent (deposits ~25%). ABCP freeze cut funding; LOLR news → first UK run since 1866. Nationalised Feb 2008.

definition: Fifth-largest US investment bank, funded ~25% by overnight repo. Counterparty haircut increases through early March 2008 created a classic repo run; Bear could not roll its funding by 13 March. JPMorgan acquired Bear on 16 March at $2/share (later raised to $10), backed by a Federal Reserve $30bn non-recourse loan against Bear's mortgage book. The first investment-bank failure of the GFC; foreshadowed Lehman.
flashcardBack: 5th-largest US IB, ~25% overnight repo. Counterparty haircuts → repo run by 13 Mar 2008. JPM bought at $10/share with $30bn Fed non-recourse loan. Lehman foreshadow.

definition: Fourth-largest US investment bank. Failed Chapter 11 bankruptcy on 15 September 2008 – $613bn liabilities, the largest US bankruptcy ever. Triggered the global panic phase of the GFC: dollar funding markets froze, the Reserve Primary MMF broke the buck the next day, Fed swap lines were activated, AIG collapsed within hours. The decision not to rescue Lehman is widely judged the worst single policy mistake of the crisis – and the catalyst for bail-in and resolution-regime reform.
flashcardBack: 15 Sept 2008 Chapter 11. $613bn liabilities – largest US bankruptcy. Triggered global panic: MMF buck-break, Fed swaps, AIG. The catalyst for resolution reform.

definition: American International Group – global insurer with a ~$440bn CDS book referencing structured-credit products. Post-Lehman, AIG faced collateral calls it could not meet. The Fed extended an $85bn rescue loan on 16 September 2008 (later expanded above $180bn), taking 79.9% equity. The intervention rescued AIG's CDS counterparties – major US and European banks – at par. Standard illustration of CDS-driven systemic interconnection.
flashcardBack: Insurer with ~$440bn CDS book. Collateral calls post-Lehman → Fed $85bn rescue (→ $180bn+) for 79.9% equity. Bailed counterparties at par. CDS-systemic illustration.

definition: French universal bank. On 9 August 2007 BNP suspended redemptions on three internal funds heavily exposed to US subprime, citing 'complete evaporation of liquidity' in some segments. The announcement froze the European ABCP market overnight; SIVs and conduits could no longer roll. Widely treated as the start of the Global Financial Crisis. The date 9 August 2007 anchors many crisis-timeline answers.
flashcardBack: 9 Aug 2007: BNP suspended redemptions on 3 subprime-exposed funds. ABCP market froze overnight. Conventional start of GFC. Date anchors timelines.

definition: US government bank-rescue programme, authorised by the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of October 2008. Initially intended to purchase toxic assets; pivoted to direct equity injections (Capital Purchase Program) into the largest US banks ($245bn deployed). Recovered the equity at a profit by 2014. Symbol of the bail-out era and the political backlash that drove the post-crisis bail-in/resolution agenda.
flashcardBack: Oct 2008 US bailout, $700bn authorised. Pivoted from toxic-asset purchase to equity injections (CPP, $245bn). Recovered at profit by 2014. Catalyst for bail-in agenda.

definition: Mid-sized US bank specialising in venture-backed tech and biotech. Failure (10 March 2023) driven by: (1) concentrated uninsured deposits (~94% above the $250k FDIC cap, in a small networked sector); (2) HTM-classified Treasury portfolio with ~$15bn unrealised losses as long rates rose; (3) a Twitter/Slack-driven run that withdrew $42bn in 24 hours. FDIC invoked the Systemic Risk Exception to guarantee all deposits; the Fed launched the BTFP. Iconic failure of HTM accounting + concentrated wholesale deposits + social-media-speed runs.
flashcardBack: 10 Mar 2023: 94% uninsured deposits + $15bn HTM Treasury losses + $42bn 24h Twitter/Slack run. SRE invoked, BTFP launched. HTM + concentration + social-media run.

definition: Sequence of Norwegian bank failures triggered by financial-sector deregulation in the early 1980s, a property and shipping boom 1985–87, and the bust that followed. Cumulative losses exceeded NOK 76bn. The state took full ownership of the three largest banks (Den norske Bank, Christiania, Fokus) – shareholders wiped out, no bail-out compensation. Standard example of effective Nordic resolution: clean nationalisation, bad-bank carve-out, eventual reprivatisation at a profit. Lessons drove the modern Norwegian regulatory architecture.
flashcardBack: 1988–93. Deregulation → property/shipping boom-bust → state took 3 largest banks (DnB, Christiania, Fokus). Shareholders zeroed. Drove modern Norwegian architecture.

definition: Wider regional collapse encompassing Norway (1988–93), Finland (1991–95) and Sweden (1990–93), with broadly common roots: financial deregulation, asset-price boom, bust, banking-system insolvency. Sweden's response – Securum and Retriva bad-bank vehicles, blanket guarantee on bank liabilities, recapitalisation with shareholder wipeout – became the international template for asset-separation tool. IMF's textbook on the crisis is on the GRA6546 reading list.
flashcardBack: 1988–95: NOR/FIN/SWE regional collapse. Sweden Securum/Retriva bad-banks + blanket guarantee + shareholder wipeout = template for asset-separation tool.

triage_reason: Merton/Marcus / FDIC – DI moral hazard story
definition: Collapse of approximately 1,000 US thrift institutions during 1986–95 with cumulative taxpayer cost ~$124bn. Causes: high interest rates compressing the spread on long fixed-rate mortgages funded with short deposits (interest-rate-risk failure); regulatory deregulation in the early 1980s expanding thrift activities into commercial real estate; flat-rate FDIC premiums (Merton-1977 trap) creating moral hazard; weak supervision allowing zombie thrifts to gamble for resurrection. Foundational example of charter-value erosion + flat-rate DI moral hazard.
flashcardBack: ~1,000 US thrifts failed, ~$124bn cost. IR-risk + deregulation + flat-rate FDIC (Merton trap) + weak supervision → zombie gambling for resurrection. Charter-value/Marcus.

definition: Unprecedented NOK depreciation and Norwegian-bond-market dislocation in mid-March 2020, in the early COVID-19 panic. EUR/NOK rose ~20% in days. Drivers identified by Norges Bank and Alstadheim's guest lecture: (1) rebalancing channel – foreign holders of NOK assets reduced exposure; (2) margining channel – FX-hedge MTM losses forced sales of NOK bonds. Norges Bank intervened with FX market support and dollar-swap-line drawing. Recurring exam question: Spring 2024 Q4b, Final 2022 Q3b.
flashcardBack: Mar 2020: EUR/NOK ~+20% in days. Rebalancing + margining channels (Norges Bank/Alstadheim). NB intervened in FX + drew Fed swap line. Spring 2024 Q4b, Final 2022 Q3b.

definition: Adair Turner's report on the regulatory response to the GFC. Six-cause framework for the crisis, cited verbatim in past grading guides: (1) macro-imbalances (global savings glut → low long rates); (2) financial innovation outpacing risk management; (3) misplaced reliance on sophisticated maths and rating models; (4) procyclicality of capital and accounting; (5) lack of confidence and runs in wholesale funding; (6) the subprime mortgage trigger. Set the agenda for Basel III, leverage-ratio backstops, and resolution reform. Spring 2024 Q3 grading guide cites the six causes verbatim.
flashcardBack: FSA 2009. Six causes: macro-imbalances / innovation / sophisticated maths / procyclicality / wholesale-funding runs / subprime trigger. Set Basel III agenda. Spring 2024 Q3 verbatim.

definition: Reg (EU) 648/2012 (refit by EMIR REFIT 2019). The EU framework for OTC derivatives, central counterparties, and trade repositories. Imposes three obligations: (1) mandatory central clearing through a CCP for standardised OTC derivatives (most IRS in major currencies, certain CDS indices); (2) bilateral risk-mitigation rules including margin posting (IM and VM under the BCBS-IOSCO 2015 framework) for non-cleared OTC derivatives; (3) reporting of all derivative trades to authorised trade repositories. FX swaps and forwards are largely exempt from mandatory clearing. The US equivalent is Dodd-Frank Title VII.
flashcardBack: EU OTC-derivatives reg (Reg 648/2012). Three pillars: mandatory CCP clearing for standardised OTC, bilateral IM+VM for non-cleared, trade reporting. FX swaps/forwards mostly exempt from clearing.

triage_reason: 2024 Q3b post-2008 reforms – listed; not deep-tested
definition: The US post-2008 framework for OTC derivatives (Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, 2010, Title VII). Mandates central clearing, exchange or SEF execution, margin requirements for uncleared swaps, and trade reporting for the US derivatives market. Administered jointly by the CFTC (swaps) and SEC (security-based swaps). Substantively similar to EMIR – both implement the G20 Pittsburgh 2009 commitments.
flashcardBack: US 2010 reform of OTC derivatives – central clearing + SEF execution + margin + reporting. CFTC/SEC. Counterpart to EU EMIR.

triage_reason: lecture 9 – not in past finals as standalone
definition: An entity that interposes itself between the buyer and seller of a derivative contract via novation, becoming the legal counterparty to both. Members face the CCP, not each other – bilateral counterparty credit risk is replaced by exposure to the CCP. The CCP collects initial margin and variation margin from members, runs a default management waterfall (defaulter's IM → defaulter's DF → CCP skin-in-the-game → mutualised member DF → cash calls), and is treated as systemically important market infrastructure under EMIR 2.2. LCH SwapClear is the dominant IRS CCP globally; Eurex Clearing, ICE Clear, and CME Clearing are major peers.
flashcardBack: Interposes via novation: buyer↔CCP↔seller. Replaces bilateral counterparty risk with concentrated exposure to CCP. Default waterfall: IM → DF → SIG → mutualised DF → cash calls.

definition: The legal substitution of one obligation for another, with consent of all parties. In OTC derivatives clearing: the original bilateral contract between two dealers is novated into two new contracts, each with the CCP as counterparty. The two original parties no longer have any legal relationship to each other; both face the CCP. Novation is the legal mechanism that lets a CCP centralise counterparty credit risk.
flashcardBack: Legal substitution of one obligation for another. In OTC clearing: original bilateral contract → two contracts vs CCP. The mechanism by which CCPs centralise counterparty risk.

triage_reason: IM concept – secondary; implicit in March 2020 question
definition: Collateral posted at the inception of a derivative trade, sized to cover potential future exposure under stress over the Margin Period of Risk (MPOR – typically 10 business days). Held by the CCP (for cleared trades) or in segregated accounts at a third-party custodian (for non-cleared, under the BCBS-IOSCO bilateral margin framework). Returned at expiry if no default occurs. Sized using historical simulation or a regulator-approved standardised model (e.g. ISDA SIMM for non-cleared bilateral).
flashcardBack: Collateral posted at trade inception covering potential future exposure under stress over MPOR (~10 days). Held by CCP or in segregated custody. Returned if no default. Sized via VaR/SIMM.

triage_reason: 2024 Q4b – VM is the mechanism behind bond fire sales
definition: Collateral exchanged daily between counterparties (or between member and CCP) based on the mark-to-market change of the derivative position. Settles realised price moves, keeping the net exposure flat. Mandatory for ALL in-scope OTC derivatives under EMIR / Dodd-Frank, whether cleared or not. The 'collateral payment when FX markets move' that drove Norwegian NBFI bond fire sales in March 2020 is the VM mechanism in action.
flashcardBack: Daily MtM-driven collateral exchange. Mandatory under EMIR/DF for all in-scope OTC, cleared or not. The mechanism behind the March 2020 NBFI bond fire sales.

triage_reason: MPOR sub-detail of IM calibration – minutiae
definition: The assumed time horizon over which a counterparty's exposure could move adversely between the last successful margin call and final close-out of a defaulted position. Used to size initial margin. Standard regulatory assumption: 10 business days for non-cleared OTC, 5 days for cleared positions at a CCP. Longer for illiquid products.
flashcardBack: Assumed close-out horizon used to size IM. Default: 10 business days non-cleared, 5 days at CCP.

definition: The fixed sequence in which a CCP absorbs losses from a clearing-member default: (1) defaulter's Initial Margin held by the CCP; (2) defaulter's Default Fund (DF) contribution; (3) CCP's own Skin-in-the-Game (a small percentage of the DF); (4) surviving members' DF contributions (mutualised); (5) capped cash calls on surviving members; (6) variation-margin haircuts or partial tear-up as last resort. Designed to make CCP insolvency extremely unlikely while limiting member exposure to mutualised loss.
flashcardBack: Defaulter IM → defaulter DF → CCP SIG → mutualised member DF → cash calls → VM haircuts/tear-up.

definition: USD risk-free rate published by the New York Fed, based on actual overnight repo transactions backed by US Treasuries. Replaced USD LIBOR after panel-bank LIBOR was discontinued – final tenors of USD LIBOR ceased on 30 June 2023. SOFR is overnight, transaction-based, and near-risk-free (no bank credit premium). Term reference rates are constructed by compounding SOFR in arrears. Legacy LIBOR contracts fell back via the ISDA fallback: SOFR + a fixed historical median spread adjustment.
flashcardBack: USD RFR replacing LIBOR (final cessation 30 June 2023). NY Fed-published, overnight repo-backed, transaction-based, near-risk-free. Compounded in arrears for term reference.

definition: An overnight interest-rate benchmark based on actual transactions in collateralised or near-risk-free markets, designed to replace LIBOR-style panel-quoted unsecured rates. Major RFRs: SOFR (USD, repo-backed), ESTR (EUR, ECB), SONIA (GBP), SARON (CHF), TONA (JPY). RFRs are overnight rates compounded in arrears for term reference – they are NOT forward-looking term rates by construction.
flashcardBack: Overnight transaction-based benchmarks replacing LIBOR. SOFR/USD, ESTR/EUR, SONIA/GBP, SARON/CHF, TONA/JPY. Compounded in arrears, NOT forward-looking.

definition: The global migration from panel-quoted LIBOR rates to transaction-based RFRs. Triggered by (i) the 2008–12 LIBOR-rigging scandals, (ii) the post-crisis collapse of unsecured interbank funding volumes that left panel banks effectively guessing, and (iii) regulatory action by the FCA. CHF, GBP, EUR, JPY LIBOR ceased end-2021; USD LIBOR final tenors ceased 30 June 2023. Legacy contracts fell back to the ISDA-defined RFR + median historical spread. The transition rebuilt swap curves, discount curves, ALM systems, and pricing models industry-wide.
flashcardBack: Migration from panel LIBOR to transaction RFRs. Drivers: rigging scandals, thin interbank market, FCA action. CHF/GBP/EUR/JPY LIBOR ceased end-2021; USD LIBOR final 30 Jun 2023.

definition: The contractual mechanism by which legacy LIBOR-referencing swaps and other ISDA-documented derivatives transition to RFR + spread on LIBOR cessation. The fallback uses the relevant RFR (e.g. SOFR for USD) plus a fixed historical median spread adjustment over a 5-year lookback ending in March 2021. Activated automatically on the cessation date for adhering parties. Solved the legacy-contract repapering problem at scale.
flashcardBack: Auto-conversion of legacy LIBOR derivatives to RFR + fixed historical median spread (5y lookback to Mar 2021) on LIBOR cessation. Avoids mass repapering.

triage_reason: DORA – not in summary, not tested
definition: EU Regulation 2022/2554, applicable from 17 January 2025. Imposes a unified ICT risk management framework on all EU financial entities (banks, investment firms, insurers, asset managers, CCPs, trade repositories, crypto-asset service providers). Five pillars: (1) ICT risk management; (2) ICT incident reporting (major incidents to authorities within tight deadlines); (3) digital operational resilience testing including TLPT (threat-led penetration testing) for significant entities; (4) ICT third-party risk – direct supervisory powers over critical cloud / IT providers via the new oversight regime; (5) information sharing. A response to the rising material role of cloud providers and cyberattacks; complements but does not replace Basel.
flashcardBack: EU Reg 2022/2554, live 17 Jan 2025. Five pillars: ICT risk mgmt / incident reporting / resilience testing (incl. TLPT) / third-party (cloud) oversight / info-sharing. Cyber-resilience for EU financial sector.

definition: The 6th Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive (EU) 2018/1673) plus the new EU regulation establishing the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA), based in Frankfurt and operational from mid-2025. AMLA directly supervises the riskiest cross-border banks for AML and CFT (Counter-Financing of Terrorism) compliance, harmonises beneficial-ownership registers, and coordinates national FIUs. KYC (Know Your Customer) due-diligence and reporting obligations are unified across the EU.
flashcardBack: EU AML overhaul: AMLD6 (2018) + AMLA in Frankfurt (live mid-2025). Direct supervision of riskiest cross-border banks; harmonised KYC/beneficial-ownership; coordinates FIUs.
